This document describes the process of installing Linkerd2 in a Kubernetes cluster. For guidance on upgrading an existing Linkerd installation, see the [Upgrade](/linkerd/linkerd2/4.2-helm-charts) section.

## Overview

Linkerd2 installation is a two-step process:

  1. Install Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs)
  2. Install the Control Plane components



These steps can be performed using either the Linkerd CLI tool or Helm charts.

Sources: [cli/cmd/install.go38-49](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/cli/cmd/install.go#L38-L49) [cli/cmd/install.go175-187](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/cli/cmd/install.go#L175-L187)

## Prerequisites

Before installing Linkerd2, ensure you have:

  * A Kubernetes cluster running a compatible version
  * The Linkerd CLI tool installed
  * `kubectl` installed and configured to access your cluster
  * Administrative access to install cluster-wide resources



## Installation Flow


Diagram: Linkerd Installation Flow

Sources: [cli/cmd/install.go90-176](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/cli/cmd/install.go#L90-L176) [cli/cmd/install.go254-261](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/cli/cmd/install.go#L254-L261) [cli/cmd/install.go262-317](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/cli/cmd/install.go#L262-L317)

### Step 1: Install CRDs

The first step installs the required Custom Resource Definitions, which define the custom resources used by Linkerd2, including:

  * ServiceProfiles
  * Policy resources (AuthorizationPolicy, HTTPRoute, etc.)
  * Gateway API resources (if enabled)




This command renders the CRD manifests and applies them to your cluster. Internally, it calls the `installCRDs` function which renders all the CRD templates.

Sources: [cli/cmd/install.go117-123](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/cli/cmd/install.go#L117-L123) [cli/cmd/install.go254-261](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/cli/cmd/install.go#L254-L261)

### Step 2: Install Control Plane

The second step installs the Linkerd control plane components:


This command renders the control plane manifests and applies them to your cluster. It calls the `installControlPlane` function which renders the control plane templates.

For production environments, Linkerd can be installed in HA mode, which deploys multiple replicas of control plane components with pod anti-affinity rules:


HA mode includes:

This page documents the Helm charts available for deploying the Linkerd service mesh and its components. Helm charts provide a template-based approach to installation and configuration management for Linkerd, offering more flexibility than the CLI-based installation process described in [Installation](/linkerd/linkerd2/4.1-installation).

## Overview of Linkerd Helm Charts

Linkerd deployment is organized into multiple Helm charts that can be installed separately or together, depending on your requirements:


Sources: [bin/helm-build67-72](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/bin/helm-build#L67-L72)

## Chart Structure and Architecture

The Linkerd Helm charts follow a modular architecture with clear dependencies:


Sources: [bin/helm-build25-48](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/bin/helm-build#L25-L48)

## Available Helm Charts

Chart Name| Purpose| Dependencies  
---|---|---  
linkerd-crds| Installs Linkerd Custom Resource Definitions| None  
linkerd-control-plane| Installs Linkerd control plane components| linkerd-crds  
linkerd2-cni| Installs Linkerd CNI plugin for transparent proxy injection| None  
linkerd-viz| Installs metrics visualization components| linkerd-control-plane  
linkerd-jaeger| Installs distributed tracing with Jaeger| linkerd-control-plane  
linkerd-multicluster| Installs multi-cluster communication components| linkerd-control-plane  
  
Sources: [bin/helm-build32-48](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/bin/helm-build#L32-L48)

## Installing Linkerd with Helm

The recommended installation process follows these steps:

  1. Install the CRDs chart first
  2. Install the control plane chart
  3. Install any desired extension charts



### Basic Installation


Sources: [bin/helm-build43](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/bin/helm-build#L43-L43)

### Control Plane Configuration

Parameter| Description| Default  
---|---|---

`controllerLogLevel`| Log level for controller components| info

Parameter| Description| Default  
---|---|---  
`proxy.image.name`| Proxy image name| cr.l5d.io/linkerd/proxy  
`proxy.image.version`| Proxy image version| install-proxy-version  
`proxy.logLevel`| Log level for proxy| warn,linkerd=info  
`proxy.resources`| Resource requests/limits for proxy| CPU: 100m, Memory: 20Mi

## High Availability Configuration

When deploying in high-availability mode, these additional configurations are applied:


Key differences in HA mode:

  * Control plane components run with 3 replicas instead of 1
  * PodDisruptionBudget limits unavailable pods to 1
  * Pod anti-affinity ensures replicas run on different nodes
  * Higher resource requests for all components

Example command with values file:

### Custom Image Registry

For environments without access to the default registry, you can configure custom image repositories:

For environments that don't allow privileged init containers, you can use the CNI plugin:

## Helm Chart Build Process

The Linkerd Helm charts are built using a dedicated script that manages dependencies and versioning:


The build process ensures that all charts are properly linted and packaged before release.

Sources: [bin/helm-build25-75](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/bin/helm-build#L25-L75)

## Relationship to CLI Installation

The `linkerd install` command actually uses the same Helm charts internally to generate Kubernetes manifests:


This ensures consistency between the two installation methods, with the CLI providing a simpler interface for basic deployments and Helm offering more customization options.

Sources: [cli/cmd/testdata/install_output.golden](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/cli/cmd/testdata/install_output.golden) [cli/cmd/testdata/install_default.golden](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/cli/cmd/testdata/install_default.golden)

## Troubleshooting

When customizing Helm installations, common issues include:

  1. **Certificate Configuration** : The identity certificates must be properly configured
  2. **Resource Constraints** : Ensure adequate resources for components, especially in production
  3. **Version Compatibility** : Charts are versioned together and should be used with matching versions



For detailed logs during installation, consider enabling debug output:


Sources: [bin/_log.sh12-16](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/bin/_log.sh#L12-L16)

## Testing Scale

When deploying with Helm in large environments, consider the scale testing script which demonstrates deployment patterns for multiple namespaces:


Sources: [bin/test-scale1-12](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/bin/test-scale#L1-L12)

## Conclusion

The Helm charts provide a flexible and powerful way to install and configure Linkerd according to your specific requirements. For more complex deployments or environments that require GitOps practices, Helm is the recommended installation method for Linkerd.

For basic installation requirements, refer to the [Installation](/linkerd/linkerd2/4.1-installation) page, which describes the CLI-based approach.

For information about how the proxy is injected into applications after installation, see the [Proxy Injection](/linkerd/linkerd2/4.3-proxy-injection) page.

Proxy injection is the mechanism by which Linkerd adds its data plane proxy sidecar containers to Kubernetes workloads. This system supports both automatic injection via mutating admission webhooks and manual injection via the CLI. The injection process modifies pod specifications to include the Linkerd proxy container, proxy-init container, and associated configuration.

For information about the proxy itself, see [Data Plane](/linkerd/linkerd2/2.2-data-plane). For policy enforcement and routing capabilities, see [Policy System](/linkerd/linkerd2/2.4-policy-system).

## Injection Methods

Linkerd provides two primary methods for proxy injection: automatic webhook-based injection and manual CLI-based injection.

### Webhook Injection Architecture


The webhook injection flow automatically intercepts pod creation requests and modifies them to include Linkerd components.

Sources: [controller/proxy-injector/webhook.go31-217](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/controller/proxy-injector/webhook.go#L31-L217) [controller/cmd/proxy-injector/main.go16-35](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/controller/cmd/proxy-injector/main.go#L16-L35)

### CLI Injection Architecture


CLI injection processes Kubernetes YAML manifests and outputs modified versions with Linkerd components injected.

Sources: [cli/cmd/inject.go50-144](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/cli/cmd/inject.go#L50-L144) [cli/cmd/inject.go154-237](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/cli/cmd/inject.go#L154-L237)

## Core Injection Components

### ResourceConfig Structure

The `ResourceConfig` struct serves as the central coordination point for injection operations:


Sources: [pkg/inject/inject.go119-154](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/pkg/inject/inject.go#L119-L154) [pkg/inject/inject.go552-567](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/pkg/inject/inject.go#L552-L567)

### Injection Process Flow


The injection process evaluates whether a resource is eligible for injection and generates appropriate patches.

Sources: [pkg/inject/inject.go678-747](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/pkg/inject/inject.go#L678-L747) [pkg/inject/report.go135-161](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/pkg/inject/report.go#L135-L161)

## Configuration Override System

### Annotation Hierarchy

Configuration precedence follows a three-level hierarchy:

Level| Source| Override Scope  
---|---|---  
1| Pod annotations| Specific pod  
2| Namespace annotations| All pods in namespace  
3| Default values| Global defaults  
  

Sources: [pkg/inject/inject.go174-189](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/pkg/inject/inject.go#L174-L189) [pkg/inject/inject.go209-550](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/pkg/inject/inject.go#L209-L550)

### Supported Configuration Annotations

The injection system supports extensive configuration through annotations:

Category| Examples  
---|---  
**Proxy Container**| `config.linkerd.io/proxy-image`, `config.linkerd.io/proxy-version`  
**Resource Limits**| `config.linkerd.io/proxy-cpu-limit`, `config.linkerd.io/proxy-memory-request`  
**Network Configuration**| `config.linkerd.io/skip-inbound-ports`, `config.linkerd.io/opaque-ports`  
**Security Settings**| `config.linkerd.io/proxy-uid`, `config.linkerd.io/default-inbound-policy`  
**Debug Features**| `config.linkerd.io/enable-debug-sidecar`, `config.linkerd.io/proxy-log-level`  
  
Sources: [pkg/k8s/labels.go124-325](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/pkg/k8s/labels.go#L124-L325) [pkg/inject/inject.go42-91](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/pkg/inject/inject.go#L42-L91)

### Injection Skip Reasons

The system provides detailed feedback when injection is skipped:

Reason| Description  
---|---  
`host_network_enabled`| Pod uses host networking  
`sidecar_already_exists`| Proxy already injected  
`unsupported_resource`| Resource type not supported  
`injection_disable_annotation_present`| Explicitly disabled via annotation  
`disabled_automount_service_account_token`| Missing service account token  
`udp_ports_enabled`| Pod exposes UDP ports

Extensions are modular add-on components that extend Linkerd's core functionality with additional features like observability, multicluster communication, and distributed tracing. Extensions are distributed as separate Helm charts and deployed into their own namespaces, allowing for independent installation, configuration, and lifecycle management.

For information about the core control plane components, see [Control Plane](/linkerd/linkerd2/2.1-control-plane). For deployment and installation procedures, see [Installation](/linkerd/linkerd2/4.1-installation).

## Extension Architecture

Extensions in Linkerd follow a consistent architectural pattern where each extension is packaged as a Helm chart and deployed into a dedicated namespace. Extensions integrate with the core control plane through standard Kubernetes mechanisms like RBAC, service discovery, and the Linkerd proxy injection system.

### Extension System Overview


Sources: [viz/charts/linkerd-viz/Chart.yaml1-21](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/viz/charts/linkerd-viz/Chart.yaml#L1-L21) [multicluster/charts/linkerd-multicluster/Chart.yaml1-21](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/multicluster/charts/linkerd-multicluster/Chart.yaml#L1-L21) [jaeger/charts/linkerd-jaeger/Chart.yaml1-21](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/jaeger/charts/linkerd-jaeger/Chart.yaml#L1-L21)

## Viz Extension

The Viz extension provides observability and visualization capabilities for Linkerd, including metrics collection, real-time traffic inspection, and a web dashboard. It is deployed in the `linkerd-viz` namespace and consists of five main components.

### Viz Extension Components


Sources: [viz/charts/linkerd-viz/templates/web.yaml1-179](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/viz/charts/linkerd-viz/templates/web.yaml#L1-L179) [viz/charts/linkerd-viz/templates/metrics-api.yaml1-172](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/viz/charts/linkerd-viz/templates/metrics-api.yaml#L1-L172) [viz/charts/linkerd-viz/templates/prometheus.yaml1-343](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/viz/charts/linkerd-viz/templates/prometheus.yaml#L1-L343) [viz/charts/linkerd-viz/templates/tap.yaml1-175](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/viz/charts/linkerd-viz/templates/tap.yaml#L1-L175) [viz/charts/linkerd-viz/templates/tap-injector.yaml1-160](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/viz/charts/linkerd-viz/templates/tap-injector.yaml#L1-L160)

### Metrics API Component

The `metrics-api` component provides a REST API for querying metrics data from Prometheus. It serves as the backend for the web dashboard and CLI commands like `linkerd viz stat` and `linkerd viz top`.

**Key Configuration:**

  * **Service:** `metrics-api.linkerd-viz.svc.cluster.local:8085`
  * **Deployment:** Single replica with `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true`
  * **Prometheus Integration:** Configurable via `prometheusUrl` or auto-configured when Prometheus is enabled



The metrics API requires cluster-wide RBAC permissions to access workload metadata across all namespaces for metric correlation.

Sources: [viz/charts/linkerd-viz/templates/metrics-api.yaml82-99](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/viz/charts/linkerd-viz/templates/metrics-api.yaml#L82-L99) [viz/charts/linkerd-viz/values.yaml89-151](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/viz/charts/linkerd-viz/values.yaml#L89-L151)

### Prometheus Component

The integrated Prometheus instance collects metrics from Linkerd proxies, control plane components, and Kubernetes infrastructure. It includes pre-configured scrape jobs for different metric sources.

**Scrape Jobs Configuration:**

  * **linkerd-proxy:** Collects metrics from all injected sidecars
  * **linkerd-controller:** Scrapes control plane admin endpoints
  * **linkerd-multicluster-controller:** Monitors multicluster components
  * **kubernetes-nodes-cadvisor:** Infrastructure metrics for Grafana dashboards




Sources: [viz/charts/linkerd-viz/templates/prometheus.yaml89-143](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/viz/charts/linkerd-viz/templates/prometheus.yaml#L89-L143) [viz/charts/linkerd-viz/values.yaml445-603](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/viz/charts/linkerd-viz/values.yaml#L445-L603)

### Tap Component

The `tap` component provides real-time traffic inspection capabilities through both a gRPC API and Kubernetes API extension. It allows users to observe live HTTP/gRPC requests and responses flowing through the mesh.

**API Integration:**

  * **gRPC Service:** `tap.linkerd-viz.svc.cluster.local:8088`
  * **Kubernetes API:** `v1alpha1.tap.linkerd.io` via APIService registration
  * **Client Access:** CLI (`linkerd viz tap`) and web dashboard



The tap service requires authentication via Kubernetes RBAC and integrates with the destination controller for workload discovery.

Sources: [viz/charts/linkerd-viz/templates/tap.yaml94-103](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/viz/charts/linkerd-viz/templates/tap.yaml#L94-L103) [viz/cmd/testdata/install_default.golden203-218](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/viz/cmd/testdata/install_default.golden#L203-L218)

### Web Dashboard Component

The `web` component serves the React-based web dashboard that provides a graphical interface for viewing metrics, topology, and performing administrative tasks.

**Dashboard Features:**

  * **Metrics Visualization:** Real-time success rates, latencies, and throughput
  * **Topology Views:** Service dependency graphs and network visualizations
  * **Administrative Functions:** Health checks, policy management, and configuration
  * **External Integrations:** Grafana and Jaeger dashboard links



Sources: [viz/charts/linkerd-viz/templates/web.yaml86-114](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/viz/charts/linkerd-viz/templates/web.yaml#L86-L114) [viz/charts/linkerd-viz/values.yaml346-410](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/viz/charts/linkerd-viz/values.yaml#L346-L410)

### Extension Values Configuration

Component| Default Registry| Key Configuration Options  
---|---|---  
`metrics-api`| `cr.l5d.io/linkerd`| `prometheusUrl`, `prometheusCredsSecret`  
`prometheus`| `prom`| `enabled`, `globalConfig`, `persistence`  
`tap`| `cr.l5d.io/linkerd`| `ignoreHeaders`, `externalSecret`  
`web`| `cr.l5d.io/linkerd`| `enforcedHostRegexp`, `restrictPrivileges`  
`tap-injector`| `cr.l5d.io/linkerd`| `namespaceSelector`, `failurePolicy`  
  
Sources: [viz/charts/linkerd-viz/values.yaml21-32](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/viz/charts/linkerd-viz/values.yaml#L21-L32) [viz/charts/linkerd-viz/values.yaml89-603](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/viz/charts/linkerd-viz/values.yaml#L89-L603)

## Multicluster Extension

The Multicluster extension enables secure communication between Linkerd clusters through service mirroring and cross-cluster identity verification. It supports both gateway-based and direct pod-to-pod communication patterns.

**Key Components:**

  * **Service Mirror Controller:** Replicates services from remote clusters
  * **Link Controller:** Manages cluster-to-cluster authentication and discovery
  * **Gateway Support:** Optional gateway-based traffic routing for non-flat networks



Sources: [multicluster/charts/linkerd-multicluster/Chart.yaml4-6](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/multicluster/charts/linkerd-multicluster/Chart.yaml#L4-L6) [CHANGES.md515-547](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/CHANGES.md#L515-L547)

## Jaeger Extension

The Jaeger extension adds distributed tracing capabilities to Linkerd using OpenTelemetry and Jaeger. It automatically instruments meshed workloads to collect and export trace data.

**Key Components:**

  * **Jaeger Injector:** Webhook that configures tracing for injected workloads
  * **OpenTelemetry Collector:** Processes and exports trace data to Jaeger
  * **Jaeger Integration:** Links with external Jaeger instances for trace visualization



Sources: [jaeger/charts/linkerd-jaeger/Chart.yaml4-6](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/jaeger/charts/linkerd-jaeger/Chart.yaml#L4-L6) [CHANGES.md352-354](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/CHANGES.md#L352-L354)

## Extension Installation

Extensions are installed using dedicated CLI commands that generate and apply Kubernetes manifests. Each extension follows a consistent installation pattern with Helm chart integration.

**Installation Commands:**

  * **Viz:** `linkerd viz install | kubectl apply -f -`
  * **Multicluster:** `linkerd multicluster install | kubectl apply -f -`
  * **Jaeger:** `linkerd jaeger install | kubectl apply -f -`



Extensions can be configured through CLI flags or by using the underlying Helm charts directly with custom values files.

Sources: [viz/cmd/testdata/install_default.golden1-13](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/viz/cmd/testdata/install_default.golden#L1-L13) [multicluster/charts/linkerd-multicluster/Chart.yaml1-21](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/multicluster/charts/linkerd-multicluster/Chart.yaml#L1-L21) [jaeger/charts/linkerd-jaeger/Chart.yaml1-21](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/jaeger/charts/linkerd-jaeger/Chart.yaml#L1-L21)

The Viz Extension provides observability components for Linkerd2, including metrics collection, traffic visualization, and real-time traffic inspection. The extension deploys to the `linkerd-viz` namespace and consists of five main components: `metrics-api`, `prometheus`, `tap`, `tap-injector`, and `web`.

## Architecture Overview

## Key Components

### Metrics API

The `metrics-api` component provides a REST API that transforms Prometheus metrics into formatted responses for the web dashboard. It acts as an abstraction layer between the dashboard and the underlying Prometheus instance.

#### Component Structure


#### Configuration Parameters

Parameter| Purpose| Default Value  
---|---|---  
`metricsAPI.replicas`| Number of replicas| `1`  
`metricsAPI.logLevel`| Log level| `defaultLogLevel`  
`metricsAPI.logFormat`| Log format| `defaultLogFormat`  
`prometheusUrl`| External Prometheus URL| `""` (uses internal)  
`prometheusCredsSecret`| Basic auth credentials for Prometheus| `""`  
  
The metrics API has cluster-wide read permissions for deployments, pods, services, and Linkerd policy resources as defined in its ClusterRole.

Sources:

  * [viz/charts/linkerd-viz/templates/metrics-api.yaml81-99](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/viz/charts/linkerd-viz/templates/metrics-api.yaml#L81-L99)

### Prometheus

The `prometheus` component collects metrics from Linkerd proxies and control plane components. It can be disabled to use an external Prometheus instance by setting `prometheus.enabled: false`.

#### Scrape Configuration


#### Default Arguments and Configuration

Parameter| Default Value| Purpose  
---|---|---  
`storage.tsdb.path`| `/data`| Data storage path  
`storage.tsdb.retention.time`| `6h`| Data retention period  
`config.file`| `/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml`| Config file location  
`prometheus.globalConfig.scrape_interval`| `10s`| Default scrape interval  
`prometheus.globalConfig.scrape_timeout`| `10s`| Default scrape timeout  
  
The Prometheus deployment mounts a `prometheus-config` ConfigMap containing the scrape configuration and uses `emptyDir` storage by default. Persistent storage can be enabled via `prometheus.persistence` configuration.

Sources:

  * [viz/charts/linkerd-viz/templates/prometheus.yaml19-164](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/viz/charts/linkerd-viz/templates/prometheus.yaml#L19-L164)

### Tap Components

The tap functionality consists of two cooperating components that enable real-time traffic inspection.

#### Tap API Server

The `tap` component provides the `tap.linkerd.io/v1alpha1` API for streaming real-time traffic data.


#### Tap Injector

The `tap-injector` is a `MutatingAdmissionWebhook` that modifies pod creation to enable tap capabilities in proxy sidecars.


#### Configuration Options

Component| Parameter| Default| Purpose  
---|---|---|---  
`tap`| `tap.replicas`| `1`| Number of tap API replicas  
`tap`| `tap.ignoreHeaders`| `[]`| Headers to ignore in tap output  
`tapInjector`| `tapInjector.replicas`| `1`| Number of injector replicas  
`tapInjector`| `tapInjector.failurePolicy`| `Ignore`| Webhook failure handling

### Web Dashboard

The `web` component provides the Linkerd dashboard interface. It serves static assets and provides API endpoints that proxy requests to the `metrics-api` and `tap` services.

#### Component Arguments and Integration


#### Dashboard Configuration Parameters

Parameter| Purpose| Default

#### Host Header Validation

The dashboard automatically generates a host validation regex that accepts:

## RBAC and Security

The Viz Extension implements granular RBAC policies for each component with separate ServiceAccounts and ClusterRoles.

### Component RBAC Structure


### Permissions Summary

Component| Key Permissions| Scope  
---|---|---  
`metrics-api`| `get`, `list`, `watch` on pods, services, deployments| Cluster-wide  
`prometheus`| `get`, `list`, `watch` on nodes, pods| Cluster-wide  
`tap`| `list`, `get`, `watch` on pods, services, namespaces| Cluster-wide  
`tap-injector`| `get`, `list`, `watch` on namespaces| Cluster-wide  
`web`| `get` on configmaps, `list` on various resources| Mixed (Role + ClusterRole)  
  
### Policy Resources

The extension includes Linkerd policy resources for secure service-to-service communication:

  * `Server` resources define service ports
  * `AuthorizationPolicy` resources control access
  * `MeshTLSAuthentication` for mTLS-based auth
  * `NetworkAuthentication` for non-mesh traffic

## Integration with External Systems

The Viz Extension can integrate with several external systems to enhance its capabilities:

### External Prometheus

Instead of using the bundled Prometheus, you can configure the Viz Extension to use an external Prometheus instance by setting the `prometheusUrl` parameter.

### Grafana Integration

You can integrate with Grafana in two ways:

  1. In-cluster Grafana: Set `grafana.url` to point to your in-cluster Grafana instance
  2. External Grafana: Set `grafana.externalUrl` to point to an external Grafana instance



### Jaeger Integration

For distributed tracing, you can integrate with Jaeger by setting the `jaegerUrl` parameter to point to your Jaeger instance.

This document covers Linkerd's multicluster extension, which enables secure communication between services across multiple Kubernetes clusters. The multicluster extension supports both gateway-based and direct pod-to-pod communication patterns for cross-cluster service discovery and traffic routing.

For general information about Linkerd extensions, see [Extensions](/linkerd/linkerd2/5-extensions). For observability features, see [Viz Extension](/linkerd/linkerd2/5.1-viz-extension).

## Overview

The multicluster extension allows Linkerd meshes running in different Kubernetes clusters to communicate securely with each other. It provides service discovery, traffic routing, and mTLS authentication across cluster boundaries through two primary modes:

  * **Gateway mode** : Traffic flows through dedicated gateway components
  * **Pod-to-pod mode** : Direct communication between pods across clusters (for flat network topologies)



The extension consists of several key components that work together to enable cross-cluster communication:


Sources: [CHANGES.md535-547](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/CHANGES.md#L535-L547) [multicluster/charts/linkerd-multicluster/Chart.yaml1-21](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/multicluster/charts/linkerd-multicluster/Chart.yaml#L1-L21)

## Architecture Components

The multicluster extension introduces several key components that handle different aspects of cross-cluster communication:

### Service Mirror Controller

The `service-mirror` controller runs in each cluster and is responsible for discovering services in remote clusters and creating corresponding mirror services locally. It supports leader election for high availability deployments.

### Link CRD

The `Link` Custom Resource Definition defines the relationship between clusters and controls how services are mirrored. Key fields include:

  * `remoteDiscoverySelector`: Controls which services get mirrored from the remote cluster
  * Gateway configuration for traffic routing
  * Authentication settings for cross-cluster mTLS



### Gateway Components

Gateway components handle traffic routing between clusters when operating in gateway mode:


Sources: [CHANGES.md541-547](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/CHANGES.md#L541-L547) [CHANGES.md665-669](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/CHANGES.md#L665-L669)

## Service Discovery Modes

The multicluster extension supports two distinct service discovery modes, controlled by the `remoteDiscoverySelector` field in the Link CRD:

### Traditional Mirror Mode

In traditional mode, the service-mirror controller creates local Endpoint resources that point to the remote cluster's gateway. Traffic flows through the gateway components.

### Remote Discovery Mode

In remote discovery mode (introduced for flat network support), the control plane performs discovery directly from the remote cluster rather than creating local Endpoints. This enables direct pod-to-pod communication across clusters:


Sources: [CHANGES.md665-669](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/CHANGES.md#L665-L669) [CHANGES.md642-647](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/CHANGES.md#L642-L647)

## High Availability and Leader Election

The service-mirror controller supports leader election to enable high availability deployments. Multiple replicas can run simultaneously, with only one active leader performing service mirroring operations:

Component| HA Support| Leader Election  
---|---|---  
service-mirror| Yes| Yes  
Gateway| Yes| No (stateless)  
  
Sources: [CHANGES.md541](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/CHANGES.md#L541-L541) [CHANGES.md750-751](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/CHANGES.md#L750-L751)

## Configuration and Deployment

The multicluster extension is deployed using Helm charts and configured through several mechanisms:

### Helm Chart Structure

The multicluster extension uses the chart located at [multicluster/charts/linkerd-multicluster/Chart.yaml1-21](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/multicluster/charts/linkerd-multicluster/Chart.yaml#L1-L21)

### CLI Commands

Key CLI commands for multicluster operations include:

  * `linkerd multicluster link`: Creates link between clusters
  * `linkerd multicluster check`: Validates multicluster configuration
  * `linkerd multicluster gateways`: Lists gateway status and metrics



### Link Resource Configuration


Sources: [CHANGES.md665-669](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/CHANGES.md#L665-L669) [CHANGES.md490](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/CHANGES.md#L490-L490) [CHANGES.md249-252](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/CHANGES.md#L249-L252)

## Integration with Control Plane

The multicluster extension integrates closely with Linkerd's control plane components:

  * **Destination Controller** : Handles service discovery for mirrored services
  * **Identity Controller** : Provides mTLS certificates for cross-cluster authentication
  * **Policy Controller** : Enforces traffic policies across cluster boundaries



The extension maintains cluster state through gauge metrics that track cluster store size and monitor the health of cross-cluster connections.

Sources: [CHANGES.md643](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/blob/adfdb340/CHANGES.md#L643-L643)

The linkerd2-proxy repository contains the transparent proxy component of Linkerd2, a service mesh for cloud-native applications. This document provides a high-level introduction to the proxy's architecture, its core components, and its role in the Linkerd service mesh ecosystem. For more detailed information about specific components, see their respective pages in this documentation.

## What is linkerd2-proxy?

linkerd2-proxy is a high-performance, lightweight service proxy written in Rust that forms the data plane of the Linkerd service mesh. It is deployed as a sidecar container alongside application containers in Kubernetes, intercepting and processing network traffic to and from the application.

Key features include:

  * Transparent proxying for HTTP, HTTP/2, and TCP protocols
  * Automatic mutual TLS (mTLS) encryption and authentication
  * Load balancing with automatic failover and retries
  * Metrics collection and export to Prometheus
  * Distributed tracing integration
  * Traffic splitting and routing based on service profiles
  * On-demand traffic inspection via the tap API



Sources: [README.md8-26](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/README.md#L8-L26)

## System Architecture

The linkerd2-proxy system is organized around a central `App` component that manages several subsystems:


Sources: [Cargo.toml6-93](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/Cargo.toml#L6-L93) [linkerd/app/core/Cargo.toml15-86](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/core/Cargo.toml#L15-L86) [linkerd/app/inbound/Cargo.toml20-46](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/Cargo.toml#L20-L46) [linkerd/app/outbound/Cargo.toml20-54](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/Cargo.toml#L20-L54)

### Code Organization

The proxy is structured as a collection of small Rust crates (libraries) to allow for independent compilation and testing. The main crates include:

Crate| Description  
---|---  
`linkerd2-proxy`| The main executable binary  
`linkerd/app`| Core application logic that binds components together  
`linkerd/app/inbound`| Handles incoming connections to the application  
`linkerd/app/outbound`| Handles outgoing connections from the application  
`linkerd/app/core`| Core infrastructure components shared by inbound and outbound  
`linkerd/app/admin`| Admin interface for metrics and diagnostics  
`linkerd/app/gateway`| Gateway functionality for handling direct connections  
`linkerd/proxy/*`| Various proxy implementation components  
`linkerd/http/*`| HTTP-specific functionality  
`linkerd/metrics`| Metrics collection and export  
`linkerd/tracing`| Distributed tracing integration  
  
Sources: [README.md62-77](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/README.md#L62-L77) [Cargo.toml6-93](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/Cargo.toml#L6-L93)

## Request Flow

The following diagram illustrates how requests flow through the proxy:


Sources: [linkerd/app/inbound/Cargo.toml20-46](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/Cargo.toml#L20-L46) [linkerd/app/outbound/Cargo.toml20-54](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/Cargo.toml#L20-L54) [linkerd/app/gateway/Cargo.toml9-22](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/gateway/Cargo.toml#L9-L22)

### Inbound Proxy

The inbound proxy handles all incoming traffic to the application:

  1. **Connection Acceptance** : Listens on configured ports and accepts incoming connections
  2. **Policy Enforcement** : Applies server-side policy rules from the control plane
  3. **Protocol Detection** : Detects whether the connection is using TLS, HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, or raw TCP
  4. **TLS Termination** : Terminates TLS connections and verifies client certificates
  5. **HTTP Router** : Routes HTTP requests to the appropriate application endpoint
  6. **TCP Forwarding** : Forwards non-HTTP connections directly to the application



Sources: [linkerd/app/inbound/Cargo.toml20-46](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/Cargo.toml#L20-L46) [linkerd/proxy/http/Cargo.toml14-62](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/proxy/http/Cargo.toml#L14-L62)

### Outbound Proxy

The outbound proxy handles all traffic from the application to external services:

  1. **Service Discovery** : Resolves service names to endpoints using DNS or the Destination service
  2. **Client Policy** : Applies routing rules based on service profiles and client policies
  3. **Logical Router** : Routes requests based on path, headers, and other attributes
  4. **Load Balancer** : Distributes requests across available endpoints
  5. **Connection Handling** : Establishes and manages connections to target services
  6. **HTTP/TCP Processing** : Applies protocol-specific processing to outbound traffic



Sources: [linkerd/app/outbound/Cargo.toml20-54](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/Cargo.toml#L20-L54) [linkerd/service-profiles/Cargo.toml12-36](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/service-profiles/Cargo.toml#L12-L36)

## Configuration and Observability

The proxy is configured primarily through environment variables and integrates several observability components:


Sources: [linkerd/metrics/Cargo.toml15-30](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/metrics/Cargo.toml#L15-L30) [linkerd/proxy/tap/Cargo.toml9-34](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/proxy/tap/Cargo.toml#L9-L34) [linkerd/opencensus/Cargo.toml9-22](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/opencensus/Cargo.toml#L9-L22)

### Metrics and Monitoring

The proxy exports detailed metrics about traffic flowing through the system, including:

  * Request volume, success rate, and latency
  * Connection count and duration
  * TCP traffic volume
  * Process statistics (memory, CPU)



These metrics are exposed via an HTTP endpoint in Prometheus format.

Sources: [linkerd/metrics/Cargo.toml15-30](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/metrics/Cargo.toml#L15-L30)

### Tracing and Logging

The proxy supports distributed tracing through OpenCensus and OpenTelemetry integrations, allowing requests to be traced across multiple services. It also provides extensive logging capabilities for debugging and monitoring.

Sources: [linkerd/opencensus/Cargo.toml9-22](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/opencensus/Cargo.toml#L9-L22)

## Service Discovery and Routing

The proxy supports multiple mechanisms for service discovery and sophisticated routing capabilities:


Sources: [linkerd/proxy/dns-resolve/Cargo.toml12-22](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/proxy/dns-resolve/Cargo.toml#L12-L22) [linkerd/proxy/api-resolve/Cargo.toml12-29](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/proxy/api-resolve/Cargo.toml#L12-L29) [linkerd/service-profiles/Cargo.toml12-36](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/service-profiles/Cargo.toml#L12-L36)

### Service Profiles

Service profiles provide a way to configure per-service routing rules, retries, timeouts, and other policies. These profiles can be defined as Kubernetes custom resources and are consumed by the proxy through the Destination API.

Sources: [linkerd/service-profiles/Cargo.toml12-36](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/service-profiles/Cargo.toml#L12-L36)

## Integration with Linkerd Control Plane

The linkerd2-proxy integrates with the Linkerd control plane through several gRPC APIs:

  * **Destination Service** : Provides service discovery and endpoint information
  * **Identity Service** : Issues and validates TLS certificates for mTLS
  * **Tap Service** : Enables on-demand traffic inspection for debugging
  * **Profile Service** : Delivers service profiles with routing configurations



The proxy is designed to operate independently if the control plane is temporarily unavailable, falling back to DNS-based service discovery and cached configurations.

Sources: [linkerd/proxy/api-resolve/Cargo.toml12-29](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/proxy/api-resolve/Cargo.toml#L12-L29) [linkerd/proxy/tap/Cargo.toml9-34](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/proxy/tap/Cargo.toml#L9-L34)

## Summary

The linkerd2-proxy is a specialized transparent proxy designed to operate as part of the Linkerd service mesh. It handles traffic interception, protocol detection, routing, load balancing, and provides extensive observability features. Its architecture separates concerns into inbound and outbound processing, with a modular design that allows for flexible configuration and extension.

For more details on specific components, please refer to the other sections in this documentation.

# Architecture

  * [linkerd/app/core/src/control.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/core/src/control.rs)

This document describes the high-level architecture of the Linkerd2 proxy, explaining the major components and their interactions. The Linkerd2 proxy is a specialized service mesh proxy that handles service-to-service communication, providing features like traffic routing, load balancing, protocol detection, and observability without requiring changes to application code.

For specific information about the inbound and outbound proxy components, see [Inbound Proxy](/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/2-inbound-proxy) and Outbound Proxy.

## Core Architecture Overview

The Linkerd2 proxy is built with a modular design around several key components that work together to process network traffic:


Sources:

  * [linkerd/app/src/lib.rs40-90](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/src/lib.rs#L40-L90)
  * [linkerd/app/core/src/lib.rs63-70](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/core/src/lib.rs#L63-L70)



The proxy is configured and launched through the `App` struct, which serves as the main entry point for the application, initializing and connecting all the components.

## Component Architecture

Each component in the proxy is structured as a composable service stack built using Tower, a library for building network applications. The service stack pattern allows each component to be built by layering multiple services on top of each other.


Sources:

  * [linkerd/app/core/src/svc.rs49-61](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/core/src/svc.rs#L49-L61)
  * [linkerd/stack/src/lib.rs49-54](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/stack/src/lib.rs#L49-L54)



The `Outbound` and `Inbound` types serve as builders for creating service stacks, progressively adding layers of functionality through a series of chained method calls.

## Proxy Processing Pipeline

The proxy handles traffic in two primary directions:


Sources:

  * [linkerd/app/inbound/src/lib.rs1-25](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/src/lib.rs#L1-L25)
  * [linkerd/app/outbound/src/lib.rs1-25](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/lib.rs#L1-L25)



### Inbound Proxy

The inbound proxy handles traffic coming from other services and destined for the local application:


Sources:

  * [linkerd/app/inbound/src/lib.rs10-17](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/src/lib.rs#L10-L17)
  * [linkerd/app/inbound/src/lib.rs63-90](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/src/lib.rs#L63-L90)



The inbound proxy accepts connections, detects the protocol being used, applies appropriate policy, and routes the traffic to the local application.

### Outbound Proxy

The outbound proxy handles traffic from the local application to other services:


Sources:

  * [linkerd/app/outbound/src/lib.rs38-50](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/lib.rs#L38-L50)
  * [linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/logical.rs1-25](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/logical.rs#L1-L25)
  * [linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/endpoint.rs71-133](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/endpoint.rs#L71-L133)



The outbound proxy discovers service information, performs protocol-specific routing, applies load balancing, and forwards traffic to the appropriate destination.

## Operating Modes

The proxy can operate in two main modes:


Sources:

  * [linkerd/app/outbound/src/ingress.rs65-97](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/ingress.rs#L65-L97)
  * [linkerd/app/gateway/src/lib.rs38-94](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/gateway/src/lib.rs#L38-L94)



### Sidecar Mode

The default mode where the proxy is deployed alongside each service, handling both inbound and outbound traffic.

### Gateway Mode

In gateway mode, the proxy can act as an entry point for traffic entering the service mesh, routing based on HTTP headers rather than original destination address.

## Service Discovery & Routing

The proxy uses a combination of service discovery mechanisms to determine how to route traffic:


Sources:

  * [linkerd/app/outbound/src/discover.rs62-148](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/discover.rs#L62-L148)
  * [linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/logical.rs74-111](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/logical.rs#L74-L111)



The discovery system resolves target addresses to concrete backends through either policies from the control plane or service profiles.

## Stack Construction

The proxy is built using a layered approach to create processing pipelines. Here's how the stack is constructed:


Sources:

  * [linkerd/app/src/lib.rs97-144](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/src/lib.rs#L97-L144)
  * [linkerd/app/src/lib.rs228-280](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/src/lib.rs#L228-L280)



The stack pattern is applied throughout the proxy, with each component composed of layers that add specific functionality.

## Control Plane Integration

The proxy integrates with the Linkerd control plane to receive configuration and policy:


Sources:

  * [linkerd/app/core/src/control.rs96-166](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/core/src/control.rs#L96-L166)
  * [linkerd/app/src/lib.rs164-219](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/src/lib.rs#L164-L219)



The proxy establishes connections to the control plane services to retrieve necessary configuration information, including service discovery data, routing policies, and identity information.

## Protocol Support and Detection

The proxy supports multiple protocols and uses a detection mechanism to identify the protocol being used:


Sources:

  * [linkerd/app/inbound/src/lib.rs237-282](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/src/lib.rs#L237-L282)
  * [linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/endpoint.rs55-69](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/endpoint.rs#L55-L69)



Protocol detection allows the proxy to apply protocol-specific processing to each connection.

## Configuration and Resource Management

The proxy is configured through environment variables and manages resources through various mechanisms:


Sources:

  * [linkerd/app/inbound/src/lib.rs41-61](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/src/lib.rs#L41-L61)
  * [linkerd/app/outbound/src/lib.rs55-86](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/lib.rs#L55-L86)
  * [linkerd/app/src/lib.rs52-71](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/src/lib.rs#L52-L71)



Configuration controls the behavior of the proxy, including connection timeout settings, protocol detection parameters, and various other operational aspects.

## Observability Architecture

The proxy provides comprehensive observability features:


Sources:

  * [linkerd/app/core/src/lib.rs16-29](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/core/src/lib.rs#L16-L29)
  * [linkerd/app/src/lib.rs312-329](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/src/lib.rs#L312-L329)



These observability features provide insights into the proxy's operation and the traffic flowing through it.

## Thread and Task Architecture

The proxy uses a multi-threaded architecture for handling various aspects of its operation:


Sources:

  * [linkerd/app/src/lib.rs404-490](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/src/lib.rs#L404-L490)



The main thread initiates the admin thread and the runtime thread pool, which handle different aspects of the proxy's operation.

## Summary

The Linkerd2 proxy architecture is built around composable services using the Tower framework. The core components—inbound proxy, outbound proxy, admin interface, and identity service—work together to provide service mesh functionality. The proxy supports multiple protocols and operating modes, with comprehensive observability features.

The proxy's modular design allows for easy extension and configuration, making it adaptable to different deployment scenarios and requirements.

Relevant source files

The Inbound Proxy is a core component of Linkerd2-proxy responsible for handling incoming connections to services. It terminates traffic from other network endpoints inbound to the local application, performing protocol detection, policy enforcement, and routing to the appropriate handlers. This document provides an overview of the Inbound Proxy's architecture, components, and request flow.

For information about how the Inbound Proxy interacts with the Outbound Proxy, see Outbound Proxy.

## Architecture Overview

The Inbound Proxy is designed as a service-oriented architecture with composable layers. It handles connection acceptance, protocol detection, policy enforcement, and request routing, all while collecting metrics and providing observability.


Sources: [linkerd/app/inbound/src/lib.rs1-40](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/src/lib.rs#L1-L40) [linkerd/app/inbound/src/lib.rs41-61](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/src/lib.rs#L41-L61) [linkerd/app/src/lib.rs40-70](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/src/lib.rs#L40-L70)

## Core Components

The Inbound Proxy is primarily implemented through the `Inbound` and associated structures:

### Inbound Structure

The `Inbound` struct is the main entry point for the inbound proxy functionality. It contains:

  * Configuration (`Config`)
  * Runtime components (metrics, identity, tap registry, etc.)
  * The service stack




Sources: [linkerd/app/inbound/src/lib.rs63-69](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/src/lib.rs#L63-L69) [linkerd/app/inbound/src/lib.rs41-61](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/src/lib.rs#L41-L61) [linkerd/app/inbound/src/lib.rs70-77](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/src/lib.rs#L70-L77)

## Service Stack Construction

The Inbound Proxy follows a composable service-oriented architecture. Services are layered to create a processing pipeline for incoming connections:

  1. The base starts with a TCP connection acceptance layer
  2. Protocol detection determines if the connection is TLS, HTTP, or raw TCP
  3. Based on the protocol, different stacks handle the connection: 
     * TLS termination and HTTP processing for HTTP connections
     * TCP forwarding for non-HTTP connections




Sources: [linkerd/app/inbound/src/lib.rs155-186](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/src/lib.rs#L155-L186) [linkerd/app/inbound/src/lib.rs236-283](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/src/lib.rs#L236-L283) [linkerd/app/core/src/svc.rs130-170](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/core/src/svc.rs#L130-L170)

## Request Processing Flow

When an incoming connection is received, it flows through the Inbound Proxy's layered services:


Sources: [linkerd/app/inbound/src/lib.rs155-235](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/src/lib.rs#L155-L235) [linkerd/app/outbound/src/ingress.rs324-344](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/ingress.rs#L324-L344)

## Protocol Detection

One of the most critical functions of the Inbound Proxy is protocol detection, which determines how to handle incoming connections:


Sources: [linkerd/app/outbound/src/ingress.rs324-339](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/ingress.rs#L324-L339) [linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/endpoint.rs179-197](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/endpoint.rs#L179-L197)

## TCP Forwarding

For connections that cannot be processed as HTTP (either because they're not HTTP or the detection fails), the Inbound Proxy provides TCP forwarding functionality:


Sources: [linkerd/app/inbound/src/lib.rs246-283](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/src/lib.rs#L246-L283)

## HTTP Processing

For HTTP connections, the Inbound Proxy provides routing, retries, and other HTTP-specific functionality:


Sources: [linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/logical.rs84-111](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/logical.rs#L84-L111) [linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/endpoint.rs72-133](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/endpoint.rs#L72-L133)

## Policy Enforcement

The Inbound Proxy enforces policies on incoming connections, such as authorization and rate limiting:


Sources: [linkerd/app/inbound/src/lib.rs121-132](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/src/lib.rs#L121-L132)

## Gateway Support

The Inbound Proxy also provides support for gateway functionality, which allows routing based on HTTP headers rather than the original destination:


Sources: [linkerd/app/outbound/src/ingress.rs65-119](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/ingress.rs#L65-L119) [linkerd/app/gateway/src/lib.rs38-94](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/gateway/src/lib.rs#L38-L94)

## Metrics and Observability

The Inbound Proxy collects metrics and provides observability features:

Metric Type| Description| Labels  
---|---|---  
Connections| Tracks accepted and active connections| direction="inbound", peer="src"  
HTTP| HTTP requests, latencies, and status codes| direction="inbound"  
TCP| TCP connections and bytes transferred| direction="inbound"  
Errors| Connection and protocol errors| direction="inbound", error="..."  
Transport| TLS handshakes and negotiated protocols| direction="inbound", tls="..."  
  
Sources: [linkerd/app/inbound/src/lib.rs159-164](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/src/lib.rs#L159-L164) [linkerd/app/src/lib.rs312-317](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/src/lib.rs#L312-L317)

## Integration with Outbound Proxy

In some cases, the Inbound Proxy needs to pass traffic to the Outbound Proxy, such as when operating in gateway mode:


Sources: [linkerd/app/gateway/src/lib.rs38-94](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/gateway/src/lib.rs#L38-L94) [linkerd/app/src/lib.rs260-274](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/src/lib.rs#L260-L274)

## Configuration

The Inbound Proxy is configured through the `Config` struct, which includes settings for timeouts, queue sizes, and policies:

Configuration| Description| Default  
---|---|---  
`allow_discovery`| Controls which endpoints can be discovered| Configured via environment  
`policy`| Policy configuration| Configured via environment  
`allowed_ips`| IPs allowed to connect| All IPs by default  
`profile_skip_timeout`| Timeout before skipping service profiles| Configured via environment  
`discovery_idle_timeout`| Timeout for idle discovery caches| Configured via environment  
`http_request_queue`| HTTP request queue configuration| Configured via environment  
`unsafe_authority_labels`| Enables unsafe authority labels| False by default  
  
Sources: [linkerd/app/inbound/src/lib.rs41-61](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/src/lib.rs#L41-L61) [linkerd/app/src/lib.rs121-132](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/src/lib.rs#L121-L132)

## Error Handling

The Inbound Proxy provides structured error handling for various failure scenarios:

Error Type| Description| Handling  
---|---|---  
`ForwardError`| Errors during TCP forwarding| Records error with server address  
`GatewayIdentityRequired`| Gateway request without required identity| Returns error response  
`GatewayDomainInvalid`| Gateway request with invalid domain| Returns error response  
`GatewayLoop`| Detected gateway routing loop| Prevents the loop and returns error  
  
Sources: [linkerd/app/inbound/src/lib.rs86-103](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/src/lib.rs#L86-L103) [linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/endpoint.rs137-176](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/endpoint.rs#L137-L176)

## Summary

The Inbound Proxy is a critical component of the Linkerd2-proxy ecosystem, handling all incoming connections to services. Its layered architecture enables protocol detection, policy enforcement, and appropriate routing for different protocols. The proxy provides extensive observability and is designed to be configurable and extensible.

title: Connection Acceptance & Protocol Detection
content:
# Connection Acceptance & Protocol Detection

Relevant source files

  * [linkerd/app/inbound/src/accept.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/src/accept.rs)
  * [linkerd/app/inbound/src/detect.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/src/detect.rs)
  * [linkerd/app/inbound/src/direct.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/src/direct.rs)
  * [linkerd/app/inbound/src/policy.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/src/policy.rs)
  * [linkerd/http/detect/src/lib.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/http/detect/src/lib.rs)
  * [linkerd/proxy/http/src/client.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/proxy/http/src/client.rs)
  * [linkerd/proxy/http/src/h2.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/proxy/http/src/h2.rs)
  * [linkerd/proxy/http/src/lib.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/proxy/http/src/lib.rs)
  * [linkerd/proxy/http/src/normalize_uri.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/proxy/http/src/normalize_uri.rs)
  * [linkerd/proxy/http/src/orig_proto.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/proxy/http/src/orig_proto.rs)
  * [linkerd/proxy/http/src/server.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/proxy/http/src/server.rs)
  * [linkerd/proxy/http/src/server/tests.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/proxy/http/src/server/tests.rs)
  * [linkerd/proxy/tap/src/grpc/server.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/proxy/tap/src/grpc/server.rs)
  * [linkerd/transport-metrics/src/sensor.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/transport-metrics/src/sensor.rs)



This document details how Linkerd2-proxy accepts incoming connections and determines the protocol being used. It focuses on the inbound proxy flow from the initial TCP connection to the determination of whether the connection is using HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, or a non-HTTP protocol.

## Overview

When a new connection arrives at the proxy, it needs to be properly classified to determine how it should be handled. The proxy must identify the connection type and protocol to apply appropriate processing, enforce security policies, and route the traffic correctly.


Sources:

  * [linkerd/app/inbound/src/accept.rs22-79](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/src/accept.rs#L22-L79)
  * [linkerd/app/inbound/src/detect.rs65-86](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/src/detect.rs#L65-L86)



## Connection Acceptance

The connection acceptance process is the first stage in handling inbound connections. It determines whether connections should be processed through the standard inbound flow or handled specially when targeting the proxy's direct port.


Sources:

  * [linkerd/app/inbound/src/accept.rs22-79](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/src/accept.rs#L22-L79)



The `Accept` struct represents an accepted connection with its important properties:
    
    
    pub(crate) struct Accept {
        client_addr: Remote<ClientAddr>,
        orig_dst_addr: OrigDstAddr,
        policy: AllowPolicy,
    }
    

When a connection is accepted, the `push_accept` function:

  1. Checks if the connection's original destination is the proxy's inbound port
  2. If so, it passes the connection to a specialized "direct" stack
  3. Otherwise, it looks up the policy for the destination
  4. Creates an `Accept` instance with the connection information
  5. Passes it to the next processing stage



Sources:

  * [linkerd/app/inbound/src/accept.rs22-79](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/src/accept.rs#L22-L79)
  * [linkerd/app/inbound/src/accept.rs13-18](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/src/accept.rs#L13-L18)



## Protocol Detection

After a connection is accepted and potentially undergoes TLS termination, the proxy needs to determine the protocol in use.


Sources:

  * [linkerd/app/inbound/src/detect.rs153-196](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/src/detect.rs#L153-L196)
  * [linkerd/http/detect/src/lib.rs153-196](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/http/detect/src/lib.rs#L153-L196)



The protocol detection process uses these key components:

  1. **TLS Detection** : First checks if the connection is using TLS based on the initial bytes
  2. **HTTP Detection** : After TLS is handled, attempts to identify the HTTP protocol by: 
     * Reading initial data (with a configurable timeout)
     * Checking for the HTTP/2 preface (`PRI * HTTP/2.0`)
     * Trying to parse as an HTTP/1.1 message
     * If neither succeeds, treating as non-HTTP TCP



The detection logic is implemented with three possible outcomes:


Sources:

  * [linkerd/http/detect/src/lib.rs25-29](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/http/detect/src/lib.rs#L25-L29)
  * [linkerd/http/detect/src/lib.rs153-196](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/http/detect/src/lib.rs#L153-L196)



### HTTP Protocol Detection Implementation

The HTTP detection implementation is intentionally designed to favor availability over strict correctness:


Key implementation details:

  1. Makes a decision based on a single read operation rather than buffering multiple reads
  2. First checks for the HTTP/2 preface as it's a simple string match
  3. Then attempts to parse as HTTP/1.1 using `httparse`
  4. If a read timeout occurs, falls back on policy hints: 
     * If policy suggested HTTP/1.1, uses that
     * Otherwise treats as opaque TCP



Sources:

  * [linkerd/http/detect/src/lib.rs31-42](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/http/detect/src/lib.rs#L31-L42)
  * [linkerd/http/detect/src/lib.rs153-196](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/http/detect/src/lib.rs#L153-L196)
  * [linkerd/app/inbound/src/detect.rs124-164](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/src/detect.rs#L124-L164)



## Policy-Based Protocol Handling

The protocol detection process is guided by policies that can influence or override the detection results.


The policy can specify the protocol to expect:

  1. `Opaque`: Skip detection and handle as TCP
  2. `Detect`: Perform full protocol detection
  3. `Http1`: Use HTTP/1.1 (but may still detect for meshed services)
  4. `Http2`/`Grpc`: Use HTTP/2
  5. `Tls`: Handle as application TLS without additional detection



Sources:

  * [linkerd/app/inbound/src/detect.rs182-206](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/src/detect.rs#L182-L206)
  * [linkerd/app/inbound/src/detect.rs242-301](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/src/detect.rs#L242-L301)
  * [linkerd/app/inbound/src/policy.rs114-123](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/src/policy.rs#L114-L123)



## Direct Connections

Connections targeting the proxy's inbound port (direct connections) are handled differently from other connections. These direct connections have special requirements:


For connections to the proxy's direct inbound port:

  1. Must use TLS with mutual authentication (mTLS)
  2. Must negotiate the transport header protocol via ALPN
  3. Transport headers must include: 
     * Target port (mandatory)
     * Optional target name (for gateway functionality)
     * Optional protocol information



Based on the transport header content, connections are processed differently:

  * With target name: Handled as gateway connections
  * With protocol info: Processed as HTTP connections
  * With only port: Forwarded as TCP connections



Sources:

  * [linkerd/app/inbound/src/direct.rs96-216](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/src/direct.rs#L96-L216)
  * [linkerd/app/inbound/src/direct.rs154-201](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/src/direct.rs#L154-L201)



## Error Handling

The connection acceptance and protocol detection processes include robust error handling to maintain proxy stability.

Error Scenario| Handling Approach  
---|---  
Read Timeout| \- If HTTP/1 policy hint: assume HTTP/1  
\- Otherwise: treat as opaque TCP  
Empty Read| Close connection with EOF error  
TLS Error| Refuse connection with specific error  
No mTLS Identity| Reject with `RefusedNoIdentity` error  
No Transport Header| Reject with `TransportHeaderRequired` error  
Policy Violation| Reject with appropriate authorization error  
  
Sources:

  * [linkerd/http/detect/src/lib.rs158-164](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/http/detect/src/lib.rs#L158-L164)
  * [linkerd/app/inbound/src/detect.rs124-164](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/src/detect.rs#L124-L164)
  * [linkerd/app/inbound/src/direct.rs227-233](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/src/direct.rs#L227-L233)
  * [linkerd/app/inbound/src/direct.rs24-29](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/src/direct.rs#L24-L29)



## HTTP Server Setup

Once the protocol is detected, connections are passed to the appropriate HTTP server implementation:


The HTTP server setup process:

  1. Creates a `ServeHttp` instance configured for the detected protocol
  2. For HTTP/1.1: 
     * Enables support for HTTP upgrades (CONNECT and WebSockets)
     * Sets up timeouts
  3. For HTTP/2: 
     * Configures flow control (adaptive or fixed windows)
     * Sets stream limits and frame sizes
     * Configures keep-alive settings



Sources:

  * [linkerd/proxy/http/src/server.rs56-126](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/proxy/http/src/server.rs#L56-L126)
  * [linkerd/proxy/http/src/server.rs131-225](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/proxy/http/src/server.rs#L131-L225)
  * [linkerd/proxy/http/src/h2.rs1-86](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/proxy/http/src/h2.rs#L1-L86)



## Conclusion

The connection acceptance and protocol detection system in Linkerd2-proxy provides a flexible foundation for handling various connection types. It balances the need for accurate protocol identification with real-world constraints, using policy configuration to guide behavior when detection is uncertain.

This system ensures that connections are properly classified and routed, enabling protocol-aware features like HTTP routing, mTLS enforcement, and observability. Its design prioritizes availability while maintaining security through strong policy enforcement.
