This page explains how the Linkerd2-proxy performs service discovery and routes traffic to upstream services. Understanding this subsystem is essential for comprehending how the proxy connects to external services, performs load balancing, and implements routing policies.

For information about inbound traffic handling, see [Inbound Proxy](/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/2-inbound-proxy). For details on the general transport layer that underlies these connections, see [Transport Layer](/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/4-transport-layer).

## Overview

The outbound service discovery and routing system is responsible for:

  1. Resolving destination addresses using DNS
  2. Applying client-side routing policies
  3. Load balancing requests across available endpoints
  4. Managing connection pools to destinations
  5. Handling retries and circuit breaking




Sources: [linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/concrete.rs1-5](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/concrete.rs#L1-L5) [linkerd/service-profiles/src/lib.rs1-46](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/service-profiles/src/lib.rs#L1-L46) [linkerd/dns/src/lib.rs1-13](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/dns/src/lib.rs#L1-L13)

## DNS Resolution

At its core, service discovery often begins with DNS resolution. The `Resolver` in `linkerd/dns` provides the foundation for translating domain names into IP addresses, which is essential for connecting to external services.

### Key Components


Sources: [linkerd/dns/src/lib.rs14-62](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/dns/src/lib.rs#L14-L62) [linkerd/app/core/src/dns.rs1-60](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/core/src/dns.rs#L1-L60)

The DNS resolution process follows a carefully designed hierarchy:

  1. **SRV Record Lookup** : First attempts to resolve SRV records, which provide both IP addresses and port information
  2. **A/AAAA Record Fallback** : If SRV resolution fails, falls back to standard A/AAAA record resolution
  3. **Negative TTL Handling** : Respects negative TTL responses to avoid excessive DNS queries
  4. **Metrics Tracking** : Records metrics on resolution successes and failures




Sources: [linkerd/dns/src/lib.rs104-138](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/dns/src/lib.rs#L104-L138) [linkerd/dns/src/lib.rs140-149](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/dns/src/lib.rs#L140-L149) [linkerd/dns/src/lib.rs151-188](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/dns/src/lib.rs#L151-L188)

### DNS Resolution API

The `resolve_addrs` method is the primary entry point, which attempts SRV resolution first and falls back to A/AAAA records if needed:


When SRV lookup fails, the proxy falls back to A/AAAA records and applies the provided default port to the resolved IP addresses.

Sources: [linkerd/dns/src/lib.rs104-138](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/dns/src/lib.rs#L104-L138)

### DNS Error Handling

DNS resolution errors are carefully managed to ensure proper backoff and retry behavior:


The error includes a `negative_ttl` method that extracts the negative TTL from either the A/AAAA record error or the SRV record error, which is used to determine how long to wait before retrying a failed resolution.

Sources: [linkerd/dns/src/lib.rs52-60](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/dns/src/lib.rs#L52-L60) [linkerd/dns/src/lib.rs202-231](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/dns/src/lib.rs#L202-L231)

## Service Profiles

Service profiles provide an additional layer of configuration for services, including HTTP routes, targets for load balancing, and protocol hints.


Sources: [linkerd/service-profiles/src/lib.rs29-46](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/service-profiles/src/lib.rs#L29-L46) [linkerd/service-profiles/src/lib.rs56-59](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/service-profiles/src/lib.rs#L56-L59) [linkerd/service-profiles/src/lib.rs77-89](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/service-profiles/src/lib.rs#L77-L89)

### Service Profile Client

Service profiles are obtained via a gRPC client that communicates with the Linkerd control plane:


Sources: [linkerd/service-profiles/src/client.rs16-20](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/service-profiles/src/client.rs#L16-L20) [linkerd/service-profiles/src/client.rs31-63](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/service-profiles/src/client.rs#L31-L63)

The `Client` struct wraps a Destination Service client and provides a method to watch for profile updates:


This allows the proxy to receive updates to service profiles without requiring a new request.

Sources: [linkerd/service-profiles/src/client.rs16-20](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/service-profiles/src/client.rs#L16-L20)

## Client Policy Routing

Client policies determine how the proxy routes requests to services. These policies can be based on various factors including HTTP headers, paths, and protocol information.


Sources: [linkerd/proxy/client-policy/src/lib.rs15-20](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/proxy/client-policy/src/lib.rs#L15-L20) [linkerd/proxy/client-policy/src/lib.rs29-44](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/proxy/client-policy/src/lib.rs#L29-L44) [linkerd/proxy/client-policy/src/lib.rs88-106](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/proxy/client-policy/src/lib.rs#L88-L106) [linkerd/proxy/client-policy/src/lib.rs109-117](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/proxy/client-policy/src/lib.rs#L109-L117)

### HTTP Routing

HTTP routing is a significant component of client policy, allowing requests to be routed based on HTTP-specific attributes like headers, paths, and methods.


Sources: [linkerd/proxy/client-policy/src/http.rs8-12](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/proxy/client-policy/src/http.rs#L8-L12) [linkerd/proxy/client-policy/src/http.rs20-36](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/proxy/client-policy/src/http.rs#L20-L36) [linkerd/proxy/client-policy/src/lib.rs72-79](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/proxy/client-policy/src/lib.rs#L72-L79)

HTTP routes support sophisticated matching rules, including:

  * Path-based matching (exact, prefix, regex)
  * Header-based matching (exact, regex)
  * Method-based matching
  * Host-based matching



And route actions including:

  * Request/response header modification
  * Request redirection
  * Failure injection (for testing)
  * Backend selection



Sources: [linkerd/proxy/client-policy/src/http.rs38-45](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/proxy/client-policy/src/http.rs#L38-L45)

## Concrete Service Resolution

Concrete service resolution is the process of resolving a logical service name to a set of physical endpoints. This process involves:

  1. Discovery of endpoints via DNS or the Destination service
  2. Application of client policies
  3. Load balancing across endpoints




Sources: [linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/concrete.rs33-45](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/concrete.rs#L33-L45) [linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/concrete.rs48-59](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/concrete.rs#L48-L59) [linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/concrete.rs73-108](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/concrete.rs#L73-L108)

### Concrete Service Dispatch Logic

The `push_http_concrete` method builds a service stack for concrete targets:


This method creates a stack that:

  1. Balances requests across a set of replicas
  2. Forwards to a single endpoint
  3. Goes into failfast mode when no services are available



Sources: [linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/concrete.rs73-108](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/concrete.rs#L73-L108)

### Dispatch Types

The `Dispatch` enum represents different ways to dispatch requests:

  * `Balance`: Load balances across multiple endpoints using the provided configuration
  * `Forward`: Forwards directly to a specific endpoint
  * `Fail`: Explicitly fails all requests with an error message



Sources: [linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/concrete.rs33-40](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/concrete.rs#L33-L40)

## End-to-End Flow

Let's examine the complete flow of service discovery and routing:


Sources: [linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/concrete.rs61-108](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/concrete.rs#L61-L108) [linkerd/service-profiles/src/client.rs63-103](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/service-profiles/src/client.rs#L63-L103) [linkerd/dns/src/lib.rs104-138](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/dns/src/lib.rs#L104-L138) [linkerd/proxy/client-policy/src/lib.rs87-106](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/proxy/client-policy/src/lib.rs#L87-L106)

## Adding a New Service Discovery Mechanism

To add a new service discovery mechanism to Linkerd2-proxy, you would need to:

  1. Implement the `Resolve` trait for your discovery mechanism
  2. Create a new `EndpointDiscovery` variant if needed
  3. Add it to the appropriate `BackendDispatcher` variant
  4. Update the client policy handling code to use your new discovery mechanism




Sources: [linkerd/proxy/dns-resolve/src/lib.rs35-64](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/proxy/dns-resolve/src/lib.rs#L35-L64)

## Conclusion

The service discovery and routing system in Linkerd2-proxy provides a robust mechanism for discovering services, applying routing policies, and load balancing traffic. By leveraging DNS resolution, service profiles, and client policies, the proxy can make intelligent routing decisions based on a wide range of criteria.

This system is designed to be extensible, allowing for new discovery mechanisms, routing rules, and load balancing algorithms to be added as needed. The combination of static configuration and dynamic updates from the control plane enables the proxy to adapt to changing service topologies without requiring restarts.

# Load Balancing & Retry

Relevant source files

  * [linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/retry.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/retry.rs)
  * [linkerd/http/retry/Cargo.toml](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/http/retry/Cargo.toml)
  * [linkerd/http/retry/src/lib.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/http/retry/src/lib.rs)
  * [linkerd/http/retry/src/peek_trailers.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/http/retry/src/peek_trailers.rs)
  * [linkerd/http/retry/src/replay.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/http/retry/src/replay.rs)
  * [linkerd/http/retry/src/replay/buffer.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/http/retry/src/replay/buffer.rs)
  * [linkerd/http/retry/src/replay/tests.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/http/retry/src/replay/tests.rs)



This document describes two critical components of the Linkerd2-proxy outbound proxy: load balancing and HTTP retry. These components work together to provide resilient and efficient distribution of requests to backend services. Load balancing distributes traffic across multiple endpoints, while retry mechanisms provide fault tolerance by automatically attempting failed requests again under certain conditions.

For information about how services are discovered, see [Service Discovery & Routing](/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/3.1-service-discovery-and-routing). For information about different modes of operation, see [Sidecar & Gateway Modes](/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/3.3-sidecar-and-gateway-modes).

## 1\. Load Balancing Overview

Load balancing in Linkerd2-proxy distributes client requests across multiple endpoints for a service. It's a critical component of the outbound proxy that ensures traffic is distributed efficiently while maintaining service reliability.


The load balancer manages a pool of backend endpoints for each service and selects the best available endpoint for each request. Linkerd2-proxy implements sophisticated load balancing algorithms that consider endpoint health, latency, and request distribution.

Sources: None of the provided files explicitly detail the load balancing implementation, but this is referenced as part of the system architecture.

## 2\. Load Balancing Algorithms

Linkerd2-proxy supports multiple load balancing algorithms:

  1. **P2C (Power of Two Choices)** \- Default algorithm that randomly picks two endpoints and selects the one with the least load
  2. **EWMA (Exponentially Weighted Moving Average)** \- Balances based on observed latency, favoring faster endpoints




The load balancing system continuously updates metrics on endpoint performance, allowing it to make informed decisions for future requests.

Sources: None of the provided files explicitly detail the load balancing algorithms, but this is standard Linkerd2-proxy functionality.

## 3\. Retry Mechanism

The retry mechanism automatically retries failed requests based on configurable policies. This improves service resilience by transparently handling transient failures.


The retry mechanism is implemented through several key components:

  1. **RetryPolicy** \- Determines when to retry requests
  2. **ReplayBody** \- Buffers and replays request bodies for retries
  3. **PeekTrailersBody** \- Examines response trailers to help classify responses
  4. **TpsBudget** \- Controls retry rates to prevent cascading failures



Sources:

  * [linkerd/http/retry/src/lib.rs26-40](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/http/retry/src/lib.rs#L26-L40)
  * [linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/retry.rs28-38](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/retry.rs#L28-L38)



## 4\. Request Buffering with ReplayBody

For a request to be retryable, its body must be preserved for potential retransmission. The `ReplayBody` component provides this functionality by buffering the request body as it's read.


The `ReplayBody` component:

  * Buffers up to 64KB of request data by default
  * Maintains shared state between the original request and retries
  * Uses efficient cloning to avoid unnecessary data duplication
  * Gracefully handles cases where the body is too large to buffer



Sources:

  * [linkerd/http/retry/src/replay.rs30-47](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/http/retry/src/replay.rs#L30-L47)
  * [linkerd/http/retry/src/replay.rs80-115](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/http/retry/src/replay.rs#L80-L115)
  * [linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/retry.rs41](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/retry.rs#L41-L41)



## 5\. Response Classification for Retries

Linkerd2-proxy uses a classification system to determine whether a response indicates a condition that should trigger a retry.


The response classification:

  * Examines HTTP status codes
  * Checks response trailers if available
  * Uses service profile configurations to determine retryable failures
  * Takes into account whether the request body was fully buffered



Sources:

  * [linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/retry.rs87-110](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/retry.rs#L87-L110)
  * [linkerd/http/retry/src/peek_trailers.rs65-86](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/http/retry/src/peek_trailers.rs#L65-L86)



## 6\. Retry Policies and Budgets

To prevent retry storms and protect downstream services, Linkerd2-proxy implements a budget-based retry limiting system.


The retry budget:

  * Uses a token bucket algorithm
  * Carefully manages retry rates to prevent overload
  * Is configured through service profiles
  * Tracks metrics for observability



Sources:

  * [linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/retry.rs114-120](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/retry.rs#L114-L120)
  * [linkerd/http/retry/src/lib.rs276-335](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/http/retry/src/lib.rs#L276-L335)



## 7\. Implementation Details

### 7.1 Retry Flow Sequence

When a request is processed through the retry middleware, it follows this sequence:

  1. Request is received and checked for a retry policy
  2. If retryable, the request body is wrapped in a `ReplayBody` with size limits
  3. Request is sent to the destination service
  4. Response is classified as success or failure
  5. For retryable failures, budget is checked and retry is attempted if available
  6. Backoff is applied between retries if configured
  7. Process repeats until success, budget exhaustion, or retry limit reached



Sources:

  * [linkerd/http/retry/src/lib.rs206-273](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/http/retry/src/lib.rs#L206-L273)
  * [linkerd/http/retry/src/lib.rs276-335](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/http/retry/src/lib.rs#L276-L335)



### 7.2 Body Buffering Internals

The `ReplayBody` component manages body buffering with several key mechanisms:


Key implementation details:

  * Uses a shared buffer model that allows efficient handling across multiple retries
  * Only buffers data that has been read from the body
  * Handles body ownership between retry attempts
  * Supports trailers in addition to data frames
  * Carefully manages body size limits to prevent unbounded memory usage



Sources:

  * [linkerd/http/retry/src/replay.rs30-75](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/http/retry/src/replay.rs#L30-L75)
  * [linkerd/http/retry/src/replay.rs162-250](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/http/retry/src/replay.rs#L162-L250)
  * [linkerd/http/retry/src/replay/buffer.rs9-17](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/http/retry/src/replay/buffer.rs#L9-L17)



### 7.3 Integration with HTTP Processing

The retry middleware integrates with the broader HTTP processing pipeline:


Integration points:

  * Works with response classifiers from service profiles
  * Integrates with metrics system for observability
  * Handles both buffered and non-buffered request paths
  * Properly manages HTTP trailers alongside body data



Sources:

  * [linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/retry.rs19-25](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/retry.rs#L19-L25)
  * [linkerd/http/retry/src/lib.rs206-273](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/http/retry/src/lib.rs#L206-L273)



## 8\. Configuration

The retry system is configured through several parameters:

Parameter| Description| Default  
---|---|---  
`max_retries`| Maximum number of retry attempts| Configurable per route  
`max_request_bytes`| Maximum bytes to buffer for retry| 64KB  
`backoff`| Optional exponential backoff configuration| Configurable  
`budget`| Token bucket configuration for retry rate limiting| Configurable  
  
Retry behavior is determined by:

  1. Service profiles that specify retry policies on routes
  2. Response classification rules defined in profiles
  3. System-wide defaults for retry limits and buffering



Sources:

  * [linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/retry.rs41](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/retry.rs#L41-L41)
  * [linkerd/http/retry/src/lib.rs43-47](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/http/retry/src/lib.rs#L43-L47)



## 9\. Metrics and Observability

The retry system exports several metrics for monitoring:

Metric| Description  
---|---  
`requests`| Total retry requests emitted  
`successes`| Successful responses to retry requests  
`limit_exceeded`| Retryable requests not sent due to retry limits  
`overflow`| Retryable requests not sent due to circuit breakers  
  
These metrics help operators understand retry behavior and diagnose issues with services.

Sources:

  * [linkerd/http/retry/src/lib.rs70-82](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/http/retry/src/lib.rs#L70-L82)
  * [linkerd/http/retry/src/lib.rs157-188](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/http/retry/src/lib.rs#L157-L188)



## 10\. Common Retry Scenarios

The retry system handles several common failure scenarios:

  1. **Transient network errors** \- Connection resets, timeouts
  2. **Server overload** \- 503 Service Unavailable responses
  3. **Rate limiting** \- 429 Too Many Requests responses
  4. **Temporary unavailability** \- Custom-defined failure conditions



The system uses response classification to determine which of these scenarios should trigger a retry.

Sources:

  * [linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/retry.rs87-110](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/retry.rs#L87-L110)

# Sidecar & Gateway Modes

Relevant source files

  * [linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/logical/policy.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/logical/policy.rs)

  * [linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/logical/policy/route/backend.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/logical/policy/route/backend.rs)
  * [linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/logical/policy/router.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/logical/policy/router.rs)
  * [linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/logical/policy/tests.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/logical/policy/tests.rs)
  * [linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/logical/profile.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/logical/profile.rs)
  * [linkerd/app/outbound/src/sidecar.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/sidecar.rs)
  * [linkerd/app/test/src/resolver/client_policy.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/test/src/resolver/client_policy.rs)



This page describes the two main operating modes of the Linkerd2 proxy's outbound component: Sidecar mode and Gateway mode. These modes determine how the proxy handles outbound connections from services in a Linkerd service mesh. For information about how the inbound proxy handles incoming connections, see [Inbound Proxy](/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/2-inbound-proxy).

## Overview

The Linkerd2 proxy can operate in two distinct modes when handling outbound traffic:

  1. **Sidecar Mode** : The default mode where the proxy runs alongside each application container, intercepting and managing all outbound connections from that application.

  2. **Gateway Mode** : A specialized mode where the proxy acts as an entry/exit point for traffic, allowing direct connection handling between different network segments.





Sources: [linkerd/app/outbound/src/sidecar.rs1-434](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/sidecar.rs#L1-L434)

## Sidecar Mode

In Sidecar mode, the Linkerd proxy runs as a companion to an application container, intercepting all outbound connections. This is the standard deployment model for service mesh scenarios, where each application has its own proxy instance.

### Sidecar Architecture

The Sidecar implementation is built around several key components that work together to handle outbound traffic:


Sources: [linkerd/app/outbound/src/sidecar.rs22-45](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/sidecar.rs#L22-L45)

The Sidecar architecture consists of:

  1. **Sidecar Target** : Represented by the `Sidecar` struct, which holds:

     * Original destination address (`OrigDstAddr`)
     * Optional service profile information (`profiles::Receiver`)
     * Policy configuration (`policy::Receiver`)
  2. **Protocol-Specific Handlers** :

     * `HttpSidecar`: Handles HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 traffic
     * `TlsSidecar`: Handles TLS traffic
     * `OpaqSidecar`: Handles opaque (non-HTTP, non-TLS) traffic



### Sidecar Configuration Flow

The `Outbound::mk_sidecar` method creates the service stack for a sidecar proxy:


Sources: [linkerd/app/outbound/src/sidecar.rs50-105](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/sidecar.rs#L50-L105)

The sidecar construction process:

  1. Creates stacks for each protocol type (opaque, TLS, HTTP)
  2. Sets up protocol detection to route connections to the appropriate stack
  3. Configures service discovery using profiles and policies
  4. Instruments connections for telemetry



## Policy-Based Routing

A core feature of the sidecar mode is policy-based routing, which allows fine-grained control over how requests are routed.

### Policy Components


Sources: [linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/logical/policy/router.rs1-303](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/logical/policy/router.rs#L1-L303) [linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/logical/policy/route.rs1-286](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/logical/policy/route.rs#L1-L286) [linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/logical/policy/route/backend.rs1-192](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/logical/policy/route/backend.rs#L1-L192)

The policy routing system consists of:

  1. **Router** : Responsible for selecting routes based on request properties
  2. **Routes** : Collections of rules that match requests
  3. **Match Conditions** : Criteria for matching requests (headers, paths, etc.)
  4. **Route Policy** : Configuration for handling matched requests
  5. **Filters** : Request/response transformations
  6. **Distribution** : Strategy for distributing requests across backends
  7. **Backends** : Concrete destinations for requests



### Backend Types

The sidecar supports different types of backends:

Backend Type| Description| Configuration  
---|---|---  
Balance P2C| Load balances requests using power-of-two-choices algorithm| Uses EWMA for load balancing metrics  
Forward| Forwards requests to a specific endpoint| Direct forwarding without balancing  
Fail| Deliberately fails requests (for testing/fault injection)| Returns configured error message  
  
Sources: [linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/logical/policy/router.rs146-167](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/logical/policy/router.rs#L146-L167)

## Gateway Mode

While Sidecar mode is the standard deployment pattern, Gateway mode allows the proxy to act as a standalone gateway for traffic entering or leaving a network segment.


Sources: [linkerd/app/outbound/src/sidecar.rs1-434](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/sidecar.rs#L1-L434)

In Gateway mode:

  1. The proxy acts as a standalone service rather than a companion to an application
  2. It still uses the same protocol detection and routing mechanisms
  3. It can receive connections directly from clients and route them to services



## Protocol Handling

Both modes use protocol-specific handlers to process different types of traffic:

### HTTP Handler

The `HttpSidecar` implementation handles HTTP traffic by:

  1. Creating route configurations based on service profiles or client policies
  2. Applying request and response filters
  3. Managing retries and timeouts
  4. Implementing advanced routing based on HTTP headers and paths




Sources: [linkerd/app/outbound/src/sidecar.rs183-290](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/sidecar.rs#L183-L290) [linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/logical/policy.rs42-85](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/logical/policy.rs#L42-L85)

### TLS and Opaque Handlers

Similar to HTTP, the proxy provides specialized handling for TLS and opaque protocols:

  * `TlsSidecar`: Handles TLS connections with policy-based routing
  * `OpaqSidecar`: Handles opaque (non-HTTP, non-TLS) traffic



Sources: [linkerd/app/outbound/src/sidecar.rs342-433](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/sidecar.rs#L342-L433)

## Comparison: Sidecar vs Gateway

Feature| Sidecar Mode| Gateway Mode  
---|---|---  
Deployment| One proxy per application container| Standalone proxy service  
Traffic Flow| Application → Sidecar → External Services| Client → Gateway → Services  
Discovery| Uses both profiles and policies| Uses both profiles and policies  
Protocol Support| HTTP, TLS, Opaque| HTTP, TLS, Opaque  
Load Balancing| Yes, with EWMA| Yes, with EWMA  
Policy Routing| Full support| Full support  
Typical Use Case| Service-to-service communication| Ingress/egress traffic handling  
  
Sources: [linkerd/app/outbound/src/sidecar.rs1-434](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/sidecar.rs#L1-L434) [linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/logical/policy.rs1-110](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/logical/policy.rs#L1-L110)

## Request Flow Comparison


Sources: [linkerd/app/outbound/src/sidecar.rs1-434](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/sidecar.rs#L1-L434) [linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/logical/policy.rs1-110](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/logical/policy.rs#L1-L110)

The key difference in request flow:

  * In Sidecar mode, requests originate from the local application
  * In Gateway mode, requests arrive from external clients



## Implementation Internals

The outbound proxy implementation uses several core types to build the service stacks:

  1. **Target Types** :

     * `Sidecar`: Holds discovery information for sidecar mode
     * `HttpSidecar`, `TlsSidecar`, `OpaqSidecar`: Protocol-specific handlers
  2. **Policy Types** :

     * `Policy<T>`: Protocol-specific policy configuration
     * `Router<T, M, F, E>`: Request routing based on match conditions
     * `Route<T, F, P>`: Route configuration with filters and backends
     * `Backend<T, F>`: Backend configuration with filters
  3. **Service Stacks** :

     * Each protocol has a specialized service stack
     * Protocol detection determines which stack to use
     * Each stack implements the appropriate routing logic



Sources: [linkerd/app/outbound/src/sidecar.rs22-45](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/sidecar.rs#L22-L45) [linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/logical/policy.rs25-29](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/logical/policy.rs#L25-L29) [linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/logical/policy/router.rs28-39](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/logical/policy/router.rs#L28-L39) [linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/logical/policy/route/backend.rs11-23](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/logical/policy/route/backend.rs#L11-L23)

## Configuration

Both sidecar and gateway modes are configured using service profiles and client policies:

  * **Service Profiles** : Define routing based on request properties
  * **Client Policies** : Configure protocol-specific policies, routes, and backends




Sources: [linkerd/app/test/src/resolver/client_policy.rs16-180](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/test/src/resolver/client_policy.rs#L16-L180) [linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/logical/profile.rs13-330](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/http/logical/profile.rs#L13-L330)

## Best Practices

When using the Linkerd2 proxy in either mode:

  1. **Sidecar Mode Recommendations** :

     * Deploy one proxy per application container
     * Configure appropriate resource limits
     * Use service profiles for application-specific routing
     * Use client policies for network-wide routing rules
  2. **Gateway Mode Recommendations** :

     * Deploy as a standalone service
     * Configure higher resource limits than sidecar
     * Use for ingress/egress traffic scenarios
     * Configure appropriate security policies



Sources: [linkerd/app/outbound/src/sidecar.rs1-434](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/sidecar.rs#L1-L434)

## Summary

The Linkerd2 proxy provides two operational modes for handling outbound traffic:

  1. **Sidecar Mode** : The standard service mesh pattern with one proxy per application
  2. **Gateway Mode** : A specialized mode for standalone proxy deployment



Both modes share the same core routing and protocol handling capabilities, but differ in deployment model and traffic flow patterns. The choice between modes depends on specific use cases and deployment requirements within the service mesh.

  * [linkerd/proxy/transport/src/listen.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/proxy/transport/src/listen.rs)
  * [linkerd/proxy/transport/src/orig_dst.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/proxy/transport/src/orig_dst.rs)



The Transport Layer in the linkerd2-proxy provides the foundation for handling TCP connections, both for inbound connections (from clients to the proxy) and outbound connections (from the proxy to target services). This document describes the core components responsible for TCP connection management, socket configuration, address handling, and original destination detection.

For information about HTTP-specific processing that builds on top of this layer, see HTTP Processing and Outbound Proxy.

## Address Types

The transport layer defines several address types to represent different aspects of network connections:

  * `ClientAddr`: Represents a client's socket address
  * `ServerAddr`: Represents a server's socket address
  * `OrigDstAddr`: Represents the original destination address for transparently proxied connections
  * `ListenAddr`: Represents an address the proxy listens on
  * `DualListenAddr`: Represents dual-stack listening (IPv4 and IPv6)
  * `Local<T>`: Wraps an address to indicate it belongs to this process
  * `Remote<T>`: Wraps an address to indicate it belongs to another process
  * `AddrPair`: Describes a connection between a client and server



Sources: [linkerd/proxy/transport/src/addrs.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/proxy/transport/src/addrs.rs) [linkerd/proxy/transport/src/lib.rs12-24](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/proxy/transport/src/lib.rs#L12-L24)

## TCP Connection Establishment

### Outbound Connections

The `ConnectTcp` struct implements the `Service` trait to establish outbound TCP connections. It takes a destination address, establishes a TCP connection, configures socket options, and returns the connected socket along with the local address.


Key features of `ConnectTcp`:

  * Establishes TCP connections to remote servers
  * Configures socket options for optimal performance
  * Returns the established connection wrapped in `ScopedIo` with address information



Sources: [linkerd/proxy/transport/src/connect.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/proxy/transport/src/connect.rs) [linkerd/app/outbound/src/tcp/connect.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/tcp/connect.rs)

### Prevention of Loopback Connections

The `PreventLoopback` wrapper prevents outbound connections on the loopback interface to avoid potential infinite loops:


This can be bypassed with the `allow-loopback` feature flag for testing purposes.

Sources: [linkerd/app/outbound/src/tcp/connect.rs15-53](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/tcp/connect.rs#L15-L53)

## TCP Listening

### Inbound Connections

The `BindTcp` struct implements the `Bind` trait to create TCP listeners. It binds to a specified address, accepts incoming connections, configures socket options, and returns a stream of accepted connections.


Key features of `BindTcp`:

  * Creates a TCP listener bound to a specified address
  * Accepts incoming connections
  * Configures each accepted connection with optimal socket options
  * Returns a stream of connections with associated address information



Sources: [linkerd/proxy/transport/src/listen.rs36-114](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/proxy/transport/src/listen.rs#L36-L114)

## Socket Configuration

The transport layer provides several functions to configure socket options:

Function| Purpose| Platform  
---|---|---  
`set_nodelay_or_warn`| Sets TCP_NODELAY to disable Nagle's algorithm, reducing latency for small writes| All  
`set_keepalive_or_warn`| Sets TCP keepalive options to detect dead connections| All  
`set_user_timeout_or_warn`| Sets TCP_USER_TIMEOUT to control how long unacknowledged data can remain before the connection is forcibly closed| Linux only  
  
Each function applies the configuration and logs a warning if it fails, rather than failing the connection.

Sources: [linkerd/proxy/transport/src/lib.rs50-99](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/proxy/transport/src/lib.rs#L50-L99)

## Original Destination Detection

The `BindWithOrigDst` struct wraps a `Bind` implementation to retrieve the original destination of transparently proxied connections:


This component is essential for transparent proxying, where connections are redirected to the proxy using iptables REDIRECT or TPROXY rules. It retrieves the original destination using the `SO_ORIGINAL_DST` socket option (on Linux) or equivalent.

Key points:

  * The `orig_dst` function retrieves the original destination address from the socket
  * Different socket options are used for IPv4 and IPv6 connections
  * The original destination is wrapped in an `OrigDstAddr` and included in the returned address information



Sources: [linkerd/proxy/transport/src/orig_dst.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/proxy/transport/src/orig_dst.rs)

## Transport Layer Integration

The transport layer components integrate with the rest of the system as follows:


The transport layer provides the foundation for both the inbound and outbound proxy components:

  * The inbound proxy uses `BindTcp` and `BindWithOrigDst` to accept connections and determine their original destination
  * The outbound proxy uses `ConnectTcp` wrapped in `PreventLoopback` to establish connections to target services



Sources: [linkerd/proxy/transport/src/lib.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/proxy/transport/src/lib.rs) [linkerd/app/outbound/src/tcp/connect.rs20-30](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/outbound/src/tcp/connect.rs#L20-L30)

## Dependencies

The transport layer relies on several external crates:

Dependency| Purpose  
---|---  
`tokio`| Async runtime and networking primitives  
`socket2`| Low-level socket operations  
`futures`| Async programming utilities  
`linkerd-io`| I/O traits and utilities  
`linkerd-stack`| Service trait implementations  
`tracing`| Logging and diagnostic information  
  
Platform-specific dependencies:

  * `libc` (Linux only): Used for system call interfaces



Sources: [linkerd/proxy/transport/Cargo.toml](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/proxy/transport/Cargo.toml)

## Summary

The transport layer in linkerd2-proxy provides a robust foundation for TCP connections with features like:

  1. Efficient connection establishment and acceptance
  2. Optimal socket configuration for performance and reliability
  3. Transparent proxying through original destination detection
  4. Prevention of loopback connections
  5. Comprehensive address type system for tracking connection information



These components work together to provide a solid foundation for the higher-level HTTP processing and routing logic in the proxy.

# Observability

Relevant source files

  * [linkerd/app/core/src/serve.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/core/src/serve.rs)
  * [linkerd/app/src/tap.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/src/tap.rs)

  * [linkerd/app/test/src/lib.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/test/src/lib.rs)
  * [linkerd/app/test/src/resolver.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/test/src/resolver.rs)
  * [linkerd/proxy/tap/src/accept.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/proxy/tap/src/accept.rs)
  * [linkerd/tracing/Cargo.toml](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/tracing/Cargo.toml)
  * [linkerd/tracing/src/access_log.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/tracing/src/access_log.rs)
  * [linkerd/tracing/src/level.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/tracing/src/level.rs)
  * [linkerd/tracing/src/lib.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/tracing/src/lib.rs)
  * [linkerd/tracing/src/stream.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/tracing/src/stream.rs)



The Linkerd2 proxy provides comprehensive observability features that enable monitoring, debugging, and understanding of service mesh traffic. This page covers the proxy's observability components, including tracing, logging, metrics collection, and traffic tap capabilities. For error handling specifics related to observability, see [Error Handling & Classification](/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/5.1-error-handling-and-classification).

## Overview

The observability system in Linkerd2-proxy collects, processes, and exposes operational data about the proxy's behavior and the traffic it handles. This data is crucial for monitoring the health of the service mesh, troubleshooting issues, and understanding the communication patterns between services.


Sources: [linkerd/tracing/src/lib.rs1-262](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/tracing/src/lib.rs#L1-L262) [linkerd/app/src/tap.rs1-133](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/src/tap.rs#L1-L133)

## Tracing System

The tracing system provides detailed information about the proxy's internal operations and the traffic flowing through it. It's built on top of the Rust `tracing` crate, which offers structured, context-aware logging.

### Configuration

The tracing system is configured through environment variables:

Environment Variable| Description| Default Value  
---|---|---  
`LINKERD2_PROXY_LOG`| Verbosity filter for log messages| `warn,linkerd=info,hickory=error`  
`LINKERD2_PROXY_LOG_FORMAT`| Format of log messages (PLAIN or JSON)| `PLAIN`  
`LINKERD2_PROXY_ACCESS_LOG`| Enables an Apache-style or JSON access log| Disabled by default  
  
The `Settings` struct in the tracing module handles the configuration of logging and provides methods for initializing the logging system based on the environment.


Sources: [linkerd/tracing/src/lib.rs25-40](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/tracing/src/lib.rs#L25-L40) [linkerd/tracing/src/lib.rs63-235](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/tracing/src/lib.rs#L63-L235)

### Log Levels and Filtering

The tracing system uses the `EnvFilter` from the `tracing-subscriber` crate to control which log messages are emitted. This filter can be dynamically changed at runtime through the `Handle` object returned when initializing the tracing system.
    
    
    linkerd=debug,warn    # Sets linkerd modules to debug, everything else to warn
    info                  # Sets everything to info level
    off                   # Disables all logging
    

The `level` module provides a `Handle` that allows runtime modification of log levels:


Sources: [linkerd/tracing/src/level.rs1-55](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/tracing/src/level.rs#L1-L55)

### Access Logging

The access logging feature provides HTTP-style access logs for traffic passing through the proxy. It supports two formats:

  1. **Apache Common Format** : A traditional HTTP server log format
  2. **JSON Format** : Structured JSON logs for machine consumption



The access logger operates as a separate layer in the tracing system, processing only events specifically targeted to it with the `_access_log` target.

Sources: [linkerd/tracing/src/access_log.rs1-166](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/tracing/src/access_log.rs#L1-L166)

### Log Streaming

When compiled with the `stream` feature, the tracing system also provides the ability to stream logs to clients through the admin interface. This allows operators to view logs in real-time without having to access the proxy's container or host.

The streaming system uses a channel-based approach, where a reader can subscribe to logs that match a specific filter. This is implemented through the `StreamHandle` and `Reader` types in the `stream` module.

Sources: [linkerd/tracing/src/stream.rs1-383](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/tracing/src/stream.rs#L1-L383)

## Tap System

The tap system allows for real-time inspection of requests passing through the proxy. It provides a gRPC API that clients can use to observe and filter traffic based on various criteria.


Sources: [linkerd/proxy/tap/src/accept.rs1-134](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/proxy/tap/src/accept.rs#L1-L134) [linkerd/app/src/tap.rs1-133](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/src/tap.rs#L1-L133)

### Tap Registry and Server

The tap system consists of two main components:

  1. **Registry** : Collects and indexes traffic events
  2. **Server** : Exposes the tap API to clients



These components are created together through the `tap::new()` function, which returns a `(Registry, Server)` tuple. The Registry is embedded in the proxy data path to observe traffic, while the Server handles external API requests.

Sources: [linkerd/app/src/tap.rs53-54](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/src/tap.rs#L53-L54)

### Security

The tap server includes security features to protect sensitive traffic data:

  1. **TLS Termination** : All connections to the tap API are secured with TLS
  2. **Client Authentication** : Clients must present a valid client certificate
  3. **Permitted Clients** : Only clients with IDs in the permitted list can access the tap data



The `AcceptPermittedClients` service enforces these security controls:


Sources: [linkerd/proxy/tap/src/accept.rs20-106](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/proxy/tap/src/accept.rs#L20-L106)

## Service Telemetry

The observability system instruments service calls to collect telemetry data throughout the proxy. This instrumentation is performed using tracing spans and events, which provide context-aware information about what's happening in the proxy.


Sources: [linkerd/app/core/src/serve.rs1-101](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/core/src/serve.rs#L1-L101)

## Testing Observability

The test framework provides utilities for testing observability components:

  1. **Mock Services** : For simulating connections and responses
  2. **IO Mocking** : For testing tracing without actual IO operations
  3. **Span Tracking** : For validating that the correct spans are created




Sources: [linkerd/app/test/src/lib.rs1-88](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/test/src/lib.rs#L1-L88) [linkerd/app/test/src/connect.rs1-134](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/test/src/connect.rs#L1-L134) [linkerd/app/test/src/resolver.rs1-304](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/test/src/resolver.rs#L1-L304)

## Integration with Other Components

The observability system is integrated throughout the proxy to provide comprehensive visibility:

  1. **Inbound Proxy** : Traces incoming connections and requests
  2. **Outbound Proxy** : Traces outgoing connections, including service discovery
  3. **Load Balancer** : Records balancer decisions and endpoint health
  4. **Admin Interface** : Exposes metrics and provides controls for tracing



Each component is instrumented with spans and events that capture relevant information about its operations, providing a complete picture of request processing through the proxy.

title: Error Handling & Classification

# Error Handling & Classification

Relevant source files

  * [linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs)
  * [linkerd/app/core/src/errors.rs](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/core/src/errors.rs)



This page documents how errors are handled and classified in the linkerd2-proxy for observability purposes. It covers the error types, error-related headers, and the classification system used to categorize HTTP/gRPC responses and errors.

For information about observability metrics derived from error classification, see [Observability](/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/5-observability).

## Error Types and Headers

The linkerd2-proxy uses a structured approach to error handling, defining specialized error types and headers for error communication.

### Core Error Types

The proxy defines several core error types:

  * `ConnectTimeout` \- Error that occurs when a connection attempt times out
  * `H2Error` \- HTTP/2 protocol-specific errors
  * `FailFastError` \- Errors when no endpoints are available
  * `LoadShedError` \- Errors when the system is shedding load due to resource constraints



### Error Headers

The proxy uses custom headers to communicate error information:

Header| Purpose  
---|---  
`l5d-proxy-connection`| Indicates the proxy connection status  
`l5d-proxy-error`| Contains detailed proxy error information  
`grpc-status`| Standard gRPC status code header  
`grpc-message`| Standard gRPC error message header  
  
### Error Utility Functions

Utility functions help with error handling and categorization:

  * `has_grpc_status()` \- Checks if an error has a specific gRPC status code
  * `code_header()` \- Converts gRPC status codes to HTTP header values



Sources: [linkerd/app/core/src/errors.rs4-56](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/core/src/errors.rs#L4-L56)

## Error Classification System

The error classification system is designed to categorize responses for observability purposes, distinguishing between successes and failures.

### Classification Components

The system consists of several key components:

  1. **Request** \- Represents the classification request configuration
  2. **Response** \- Handles initial response classification
  3. **Eos** (End of Stream) - Handles classification with HTTP trailers
  4. **Class** \- The final classification result



### Classification Process

The classification process flows through these components:

  1. A `Request` classifies an HTTP request based on its properties
  2. The resulting `Response` classifier processes the HTTP response
  3. The `Eos` (End of Stream) processor handles trailers and stream completion
  4. A final `Class` is produced that categorizes the response as success or failure



Sources: [linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs1-39](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs#L1-L39) [linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs40-204](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs#L40-L204)

## Request Classification

The `Request` enum defines how requests should be classified:
    
    
    Request {
      Default,                        // Use default classification rules
      Profile(ResponseClasses),       // Use rules from a service profile
      ClientPolicy(ClientPolicy),     // Use rules from a client policy
    }
    

When a request is classified, it produces a `Response` object configured to classify the corresponding HTTP/gRPC response.

Sources: [linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs12-17](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs#L12-L17) [linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs65-90](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs#L65-L90)

## Response Classification

The `Response` enum determines how HTTP/gRPC responses are classified:
    
    
    Response {
      Http(StatusRanges),             // HTTP status code-based classification
      Grpc(Codes),                    // gRPC status code-based classification
      Profile(ResponseClasses),       // Service profile-based classification
    }
    

The classification logic varies depending on protocol:

  * **HTTP responses** are classified primarily by their status code:

    * 5xx status codes are generally classified as failures
    * Others are classified based on configurable status ranges
  * **gRPC responses** are classified by their status codes from trailers or headers:

    * Code 0 (OK) is classified as success
    * Codes like UNAVAILABLE, INTERNAL, etc. are classified as failures
    * Other codes are classified based on configurable code ranges



Sources: [linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs18-24](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs#L18-L24) [linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs100-167](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs#L100-L167)

## End of Stream Classification

The `Eos` enum handles classification of completed streams, which is especially important for gRPC where status codes often appear in trailers:
    
    
    Eos {
      Class(Class),                   // Final classification
      GrpcOpen(Codes),                // gRPC stream waiting for trailers
      ProfileUnmatched(Class),        // Didn't match profile rules
    }
    

This component processes HTTP trailers and converts them to a final classification result.

Sources: [linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs32-37](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs#L32-L37) [linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs171-204](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs#L171-L204)

## Classification Result

The `Class` enum represents the final classification result:
    
    
    Class {
      Http(Result<StatusCode>),       // HTTP success or failure
      Grpc(Result<Code>),             // gRPC success or failure
      Error(String),                  // Generic error
    }
    

The `Result` wrapper indicates success (Ok) or failure (Err). The system uses this information to:

  * Increment appropriate metrics
  * Log with appropriate severity
  * Include in tracing information



Sources: [linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs41-45](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs#L41-L45) [linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs232-246](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs#L232-L246)

## Error Handling Workflow

The following diagram illustrates the error handling and classification process:


Sources: [linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs65-90](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs#L65-L90) [linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs120-167](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs#L120-L167) [linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs171-204](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs#L171-L204)

## HTTP Error Classification

HTTP errors are classified based on status codes and custom rules:


This classification approach allows for:

  * Default handling of common status codes
  * Custom classification through service profiles
  * Distinguishing between client and server errors



Sources: [linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs100-117](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs#L100-L117) [linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs248-282](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs#L248-L282)

## gRPC Error Classification

gRPC errors are classified based on status codes found in headers or trailers:


By default, these gRPC codes are classified as failures:

  * UNKNOWN (2)
  * DEADLINE_EXCEEDED (4)
  * RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED (8)
  * INTERNAL (13)
  * UNAVAILABLE (14)



Sources: [linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs133-137](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs#L133-L137) [linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs171-197](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs#L171-L197) [linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs284-342](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs#L284-L342)

## Code Entity to System Component Mapping

The following diagram maps code entities to system components:


Sources: [linkerd/app/core/src/errors.rs4-22](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/core/src/errors.rs#L4-L22) [linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs10-45](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs#L10-L45)

## Error Classification in Headers and Trailers

The following table shows how error classification information is communicated in HTTP headers and trailers:

Header/Trailer| Format| Purpose  
---|---|---  
`l5d-proxy-error`| String| Describes proxy-generated errors  
`grpc-status`| Numeric code (0-16)| Standard gRPC status code  
`grpc-message`| String| Human-readable gRPC error message  
  
The proxy uses these headers to:

  1. Communicate error information to clients
  2. Extract error information from upstream services
  3. Classify responses for metrics and logging



Sources: [linkerd/app/core/src/errors.rs10-18](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/core/src/errors.rs#L10-L18) [linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs206-211](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs#L206-L211)

## Testing Error Classification

The proxy includes comprehensive tests for error classification, ensuring that:

  * HTTP status codes are correctly classified
  * gRPC status codes in headers are correctly classified
  * gRPC status codes in trailers are correctly classified
  * Different combinations of headers and trailers are handled correctly



These tests validate that the classification system works correctly across different protocols and response patterns.

Sources: [linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs248-388](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/core/src/classify.rs#L248-L388)

In summary, the linkerd2-proxy's error handling and classification system provides a robust framework for:

  1. Handling errors consistently across different protocols
  2. Classifying responses as successes or failures
  3. Providing detailed error information for observability
  4. Supporting custom classification through service profiles and client policies

This document describes the configuration system for the Linkerd2 proxy, explaining how the proxy is configured through environment variables, the primary configuration structures, and important configuration options.

## Overview

The Linkerd2 proxy is primarily configured through environment variables. At startup, the proxy reads these variables and constructs a comprehensive configuration object that controls all aspects of its behavior, from networking parameters to performance tuning.


Sources:

  * [linkerd/app/src/env.rs28-37](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/src/env.rs#L28-L37)
  * [linkerd/app/src/env.rs364-453](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/src/env.rs#L364-L453)



## Configuration Loading Process

The configuration loading process begins with the `Strings` trait, which provides an interface for retrieving string values by key:


Sources:

  * [linkerd/app/src/env.rs28-37](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/src/env.rs#L28-L37)
  * [linkerd/app/src/env.rs364-841](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/src/env.rs#L364-L841)



The `parse_config` function in `linkerd/app/src/env.rs` orchestrates the loading of all configuration components. It uses helper functions to parse individual environment variables into the appropriate types, handling errors and applying default values when needed.

## Core Configuration Structures

The proxy's configuration is organized into a hierarchy of structures, each responsible for a specific aspect of the proxy:


Sources:

  * [linkerd/app/core/src/config.rs9-44](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/core/src/config.rs#L9-L44)
  * [linkerd/app/src/env.rs595-745](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/src/env.rs#L595-L745) (inbound config)
  * [linkerd/app/src/env.rs487-586](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/src/env.rs#L487-L586) (outbound config)



### Key Configuration Components

  1. **ServerConfig** : Controls how the proxy listens for incoming connections

     * Listen address and port
     * TCP keepalive settings
     * TCP user timeout settings
     * HTTP/2 server parameters
  2. **ConnectConfig** : Controls how the proxy connects to upstream servers

     * Connection timeout
     * Backoff policy for retries
     * Keepalive settings
     * HTTP/1 connection pool settings
     * HTTP/2 client parameters
  3. **QueueConfig** : Controls buffering and backpressure

     * Queue capacity (number of requests/connections that can be buffered)
     * Failfast timeout (how long requests can wait in the queue)
  4. **ProxyConfig** : Combines server and connect configurations with proxy-specific settings

     * Server configuration
     * Connect configuration
     * Maximum in-flight requests
     * Protocol detection timeout



Sources:

  * [linkerd/app/core/src/config.rs9-33](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/core/src/config.rs#L9-L33)



## Environment Variables

The proxy is configured through a large set of environment variables. These are defined as constants in `linkerd/app/src/env.rs`:


Sources:

### Important Environment Variables

LINKERD2_PROXY_OUTBOUND_LISTEN_ADDR| Address where the proxy listens for outbound connections| 127.0.0.1:4140  
LINKERD2_PROXY_CONTROL_LISTEN_ADDR| Address where the proxy listens for control plane connections| 0.0.0.0:4190  
LINKERD2_PROXY_ADMIN_LISTEN_ADDR| Address where the proxy listens for admin connections| 127.0.0.1:4191  
LINKERD2_PROXY_INBOUND_CONNECT_TIMEOUT| Timeout for inbound connections to upstream services| 300ms  
LINKERD2_PROXY_OUTBOUND_CONNECT_TIMEOUT| Timeout for outbound connections to upstream services| 1s  
LINKERD2_PROXY_INBOUND_DETECT_TIMEOUT| Timeout for inbound protocol detection| 10s  
LINKERD2_PROXY_OUTBOUND_DETECT_TIMEOUT| Timeout for outbound protocol detection| 10s  
LINKERD2_PROXY_INBOUND_MAX_IN_FLIGHT| Maximum number of in-flight inbound requests| 100,000  
LINKERD2_PROXY_OUTBOUND_MAX_IN_FLIGHT| Maximum number of in-flight outbound requests| 100,000

## Default Configuration

## Specialized Configuration Areas

### HTTP/2 Configuration

HTTP/2 settings can be tuned for both client and server connections:

### Inbound Policy Configuration

Inbound policy controls how the proxy handles incoming connections:


Sources:

  * [linkerd/app/src/env.rs193-207](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/src/env.rs#L193-L207)
  * [linkerd/app/src/env.rs659-720](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/src/env.rs#L659-L720)



### Service Discovery Configuration

The proxy can be configured to discover services using the Destination service:


Sources:

  * [linkerd/app/src/env.rs165-184](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/src/env.rs#L165-L184)

## Configuration Impact on Proxy Behavior

The configuration directly impacts how the proxy behaves at runtime. Key areas affected include:

  1. **Connection Management**

     * Connection timeouts and keepalive settings affect resource usage and resilience
     * Queue capacities and failfast timeouts affect backpressure and overload handling
  2. **Protocol Detection**

     * Protocol detection timeouts determine how quickly the proxy identifies protocols
     * Disabling protocol detection for specific ports can optimize performance
  3. **Service Discovery**

     * Profile suffixes and networks control which services are discovered via the Destination service
     * Discovery idle timeouts control how long service information is cached
  4. **Resource Utilization**

     * HTTP connection pool settings control connection reuse
     * Max in-flight requests limit concurrent request processing



Sources:

  * [linkerd/app/inbound/src/http/router.rs175-252](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/inbound/src/http/router.rs#L175-L252)
  * [linkerd/app/admin/src/stack.rs75-209](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/linkerd/app/admin/src/stack.rs#L75-L209)

Test utilities demonstrate how to construct valid configurations programmatically:

## Conclusion

The Linkerd2 proxy's configuration system is comprehensive and flexible, allowing detailed control over proxy behavior through environment variables. The system provides sensible defaults while enabling fine-grained customization for specific deployment scenarios and requirements.

This page provides information for developers who want to work on the linkerd2-proxy codebase. It covers development environment setup, building the project, development workflow, and contribution guidelines. For specific information about the build system, see [Build System](/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/7.1-build-system), for testing methodologies, see [Testing & Fuzzing](/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/7.2-testing-and-fuzzing), and for CI/CD details, see [CI/CD Pipeline](/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/7.3-cicd-pipeline).

## Development Environment Setup

The linkerd2-proxy project supports multiple development environment options, with the recommended approach being a Dev Container setup.

### Development Container

The project provides a Dev Container configuration that works with VS Code and other compatible tools. This container has all the necessary tools and dependencies pre-installed for building and testing the proxy.


The Dev Container is configured with:

  * Memory limits (24GB)
  * Host network access
  * Docker socket access
  * Necessary capabilities for debugging
  * Rust flags for tokio unstable features
  * C++ compiler configuration



Sources: [.devcontainer/devcontainer.json1-63](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/.devcontainer/devcontainer.json#L1-L63) [.devcontainer/Dockerfile1-13](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/.devcontainer/Dockerfile#L1-L13)

### Local Development Environment

If you prefer to develop without using the Dev Container, you'll need to install the required tools manually:


The `RUSTFLAGS="--cfg tokio_unstable"` environment variable is recommended for enabling tokio's unstable features used in the codebase.

Sources: [README.md33-59](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/README.md#L33-L59) [.devcontainer/devcontainer.json52-54](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/.devcontainer/devcontainer.json#L52-L54)

## Building the Project

The project uses a combination of `just` (a command runner) and `cargo` (Rust's package manager) for building and testing. The project provides a wrapper around these tools called `just-cargo`.

### Using Just

The project includes a `justfile` that defines common development tasks:


Common just commands:

  * `just build` \- Compiles the proxy locally using cargo
  * `just test` \- Runs unit and integration tests
  * `just docker` \- Builds a Docker container image for testing



Sources: [README.md42-49](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/README.md#L42-L49)

### Repository Structure

The project is organized as a collection of many small crates to enable independent compilation and testing of components:


This modular structure allows components to be compiled and tested independently, which improves development workflow efficiency.

Sources: [README.md61-77](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/README.md#L61-L77)

## Development Workflow

The typical development workflow involves making changes, testing them locally, and then submitting a pull request.


Sources: [CONTRIBUTING.md29-42](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/CONTRIBUTING.md#L29-L42)

## Code Contribution Guidelines

### Commit Messages

Commit messages should follow this format:
    
    
    Subject
    
    Problem
    
    Solution
    
    Validation
    
    Fixes #[GitHub issue ID]
    

Where:

  * Subject is one line, ≤ 50 characters, describes what is done
  * Problem explains the context and motivation
  * Solution describes the modifications made
  * Validation describes testing done to validate the change



Sources: [CONTRIBUTING.md44-100](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/CONTRIBUTING.md#L44-L100)

### Developer Certificate of Origin

All contributions require a Developer Certificate of Origin (DCO) sign-off. This is a simple line added to each commit message:
    
    
    Signed-off-by: Jane Smith <jane.smith@example.com>
    

You can automatically add this by using `git commit -s` if your user.name and user.email are properly configured.

Sources: [CONTRIBUTING.md11-27](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/CONTRIBUTING.md#L11-L27) [DCO1-38](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/DCO#L1-L38)

## Fuzzing

The project uses fuzzing as part of its security testing strategy. Fuzzing tests are organized within the directories of the crates they test.


Fuzz tests are wrapped with `#[cfg(fuzzing)]` to avoid including them in release builds.

To run a fuzzer locally:

  1. Navigate to the crate directory (e.g., `cd linkerd/addr`)
  2. Build with `cargo +nightly fuzz build`
  3. Run with `./fuzz/target/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/release/fuzz_target_1`



Sources: [docs/FUZZING.md1-102](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/docs/FUZZING.md#L1-L102)

## Getting Help

If you encounter issues or have questions while developing for linkerd2-proxy, you can:

  * Ask questions in the forums at <https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2/discussions>
  * Join the #linkerd2 Slack channel
  * Open an issue in the GitHub repository



Sources: [CONTRIBUTING.md5-9](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/CONTRIBUTING.md#L5-L9)

## Purpose and Scope

This document details the build system used for the Linkerd2-proxy repository. It covers the tools, configuration, and processes used to build, test, and package the proxy. For information about the CI/CD pipeline, see [CI/CD Pipeline](/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/7.3-cicd-pipeline), and for details on testing, refer to [Testing & Fuzzing](/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/7.2-testing-and-fuzzing).

## Build Tools Overview

The Linkerd2-proxy build system relies on several key tools that work together to create optimized builds for various target environments.


Sources: [README.md34-48](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/README.md#L34-L48) [Dockerfile1-55](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/Dockerfile#L1-L55)

### Cargo

Cargo is Rust's package manager and build tool. It handles dependency management, compilation, and testing for the project. The Linkerd2-proxy codebase is organized into multiple Rust crates that Cargo manages.

### Just

The project uses `just`, a command runner similar to `make`, to automate build tasks. The `justfile` at the root of the repository defines recipes for common development tasks:

  * `just build` \- Compiles the proxy locally using Cargo
  * `just test` \- Runs unit and integration tests
  * `just docker` \- Builds a Docker container image



The project also uses a thin wrapper around just and cargo called `just-cargo`.

Sources: [README.md34-48](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/README.md#L34-L48)

### Docker

Docker is used to build container images of the proxy. The `Dockerfile` defines a multi-stage build process that:

  1. Uses a base Rust image for development
  2. Fetches dependencies
  3. Builds the proxy with specified features and profiles
  4. Creates a minimal runtime image with the built proxy



Sources: [Dockerfile1-55](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/Dockerfile#L1-L55)

### Dev Container

A development container configuration is provided for Visual Studio Code users. It includes all necessary tooling for building and testing the proxy, allowing developers to avoid setting up the complex development environment manually.

Sources: [README.md38-39](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/README.md#L38-L39) [README.md56-59](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/README.md#L56-L59)

## Build Process

The build process varies depending on whether you're building locally or using Docker, and whether it's for development or production.


Sources: [Dockerfile12-55](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/Dockerfile#L12-L55) [README.md42-49](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/README.md#L42-L49)

### Local Development Build

For local development:

  1. Run `just build` to compile the proxy
  2. The binary is generated in the target directory based on the selected profile (debug or release)



### Docker Build

The Docker build defined in the `Dockerfile` uses a multi-stage process:

  1. **Fetch Stage** : Using a Rust base image, it copies the source code and fetches dependencies
         
         FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM $RUST_IMAGE as fetch
         

  2. **Build Stage** : Compiles the proxy with specified features, profile, and target architecture
         
         FROM fetch as build
         

     * Controlled by build arguments like: 
       * `PROXY_FEATURES`: Optional features to enable
       * `PROFILE`: Build profile (debug or release)
       * `TARGETARCH`: Target architecture
  3. **Runtime Stage** : Creates a minimal Debian-based image with the compiled proxy
         
         FROM docker.io/library/debian:bookworm-slim as runtime
         




Sources: [Dockerfile12-55](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/Dockerfile#L12-L55)

## Build Configuration

Several configuration mechanisms control how the proxy is built:

### Environment Variables

The build process uses various environment variables:

  * `CARGO_INCREMENTAL`: Controls incremental compilation
  * `RUSTFLAGS`: Configures Rust compiler flags
  * `CARGO_NET_RETRY` and `RUSTUP_MAX_RETRIES`: Control network retry behavior




Sources: [Dockerfile24-25](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/Dockerfile#L24-L25) [Dockerfile34-39](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/Dockerfile#L34-L39)

### Build Arguments

Docker build arguments provide another layer of configuration:

  * `RUST_IMAGE`: Base image for Rust compilation
  * `LINKERD2_IMAGE`: Image containing identity-initializing and linkerd-await wrappers
  * `PROFILE`: Build profile (debug or release)
  * `TARGETARCH`: Target architecture for the build
  * `LINKERD2_PROXY_VERSION` and `LINKERD2_PROXY_VENDOR`: Version information



### Feature Flags

The `PROXY_FEATURES` build argument allows enabling optional features, such as:

  * `meshtls-boring`: Uses BoringSSL for TLS (requires golang)
  * `pprof`: Enables profiling support



Sources: [Dockerfile16-22](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/Dockerfile#L16-L22) [Dockerfile41-46](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/Dockerfile#L41-L46)

## Repository Structure

The project is structured into many small libraries (crates) to enable independent compilation and testing.


Key crates include:

  * **linkerd2-proxy** : Contains the proxy executable
  * **linkerd2-app** : Bundles the inbound and outbound crates
  * **linkerd2-app-inbound** : Handles incoming connections
  * **linkerd2-app-outbound** : Handles outgoing connections
  * **linkerd2-app-integration** : Contains integration tests



Sources: [README.md61-71](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/README.md#L61-L71)

## Caching Mechanism

The build system uses caching to speed up builds:

  * Docker's cache mounting for the Cargo registry: 
        
        RUN --mount=type=cache,id=cargo,target=/usr/local/cargo/registry
        

  * This significantly reduces build times by preserving downloaded dependencies between builds



Sources: [Dockerfile29-30](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/Dockerfile#L29-L30) [Dockerfile41-46](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/Dockerfile#L41-L46)

## Development Workflow


For local development, the recommended workflow is:

  1. Use the Dev Container to set up your development environment
  2. Edit the source code
  3. Use `just build` to compile the project
  4. Use `just test` to run tests
  5. Use `just docker` to build a Docker image for testing



Sources: [README.md34-59](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/README.md#L34-L59)

## Summary

The Linkerd2-proxy build system combines Rust's Cargo, the Just command runner, and Docker to provide a flexible and powerful build environment. By using multi-stage Docker builds and caching mechanisms, it optimizes both development experience and production builds.

The repository's structure into multiple crates enables modular development and testing, while the various configuration options allow for customizing builds according to different requirements and target environments.

Sources: [README.md34-71](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/README.md#L34-L71) [Dockerfile1-55](https://github.com/linkerd/linkerd2-proxy/blob/ff162dba/Dockerfile#L1-L55)
